o4xfbf.text: The PHP security team is warning administrators to prepare for emergency security updates tomorrow to address two critical vulnerabilities, as information about the flaws has reportedly leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. PHP powers many websites and web applications, including content management systems, e-commerce platforms, and custom web services. In an advisory published Tuesday, the PHP development team announced that it plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern), to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. The PHP security team also sent a notice to its ANNOUNCE mailing list, urging administrators to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they become available. "We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild," the PHP security team warned. The developers have not disclosed any technical details about the vulnerabilities, including which PHP versions are affected, how they can be exploited, or which releases will contain fixes. However, security researchers at watchTowr told BleepingComputer that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are remote code execution (RCE) flaws believed to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. "In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET," watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris told BleepingComputer. "While we are not able to share technical information at this point for obvious reasons, given the sensitivity, we can confirm that these vulnerabilities are indeed real. Both of them are CVSS10 and are understood to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8." watchTowr also said it believes it has successfully reproduced CVE-2026-109618 but is not releasing technical information until security patches become available. The researchers clarified that they have not observed exploitation of the vulnerabilities in the wild, despite the information reportedly leaking ahead of the planned disclosure. In a post on X, watchTowr warned that information about the vulnerabilities had leaked before the originally planned disclosure date. "We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real," the researchers said. The warning follows a now-deleted post on Y Combinator's Hacker News forum, in which a user named "petecooper" claimed that two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22. The post, seen by BleepingComputer, claimed that both vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 10.0 and affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5. It also identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, matching the identifiers watchTowr later shared. However, watchTowr's statements and the Hacker News post are different from PHP's official announcement. Both described the vulnerabilities as CVSS 10.0, while the PHP security team assigned each a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Additionally, watchTowr cited an originally planned Thursday disclosure, while PHP has officially scheduled its security release for tomorrow morning. The PHP security team says it will publish full technical details, affected versions, and fixed releases when the security updates become available. f10pjy.text: At least 600 organizations across the U.S. and Europe have been breached by the SafePay ransomware gang since August 2024, according to a new advisory from international law enforcement agencies. The FBI and cybersecurity agencies in Germany as well as the U.K. said SafePay is now “among the most active ransomware groups in 2026” and is targeting businesses and critical infrastructure by guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities and using phishing attacks. The advisory was created based on numerous FBI and German law enforcement investigations involving SafePay, with the most recent incident occurring in August. The advisory lists multiple vulnerabilities the group has used in attacks, including CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2023-20269, CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, CVE-2024-40766 and others. “Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones,” the agencies said. “They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection.” The group also uses automated scripts to target vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems. In some cases, the hackers change the passwords of system users to make it harder for them to login and stop their activity. They use legitimate tools to compress files and exfiltrate them before deploying the ransomware on victim devices. Legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer are used to transfer ransomware onto victim systems. The advisory said SafePay typically holds encrypted data for ransom and demands “a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency” in exchange for the decryption key. “To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group.” The group’s leak site currently lists dozens of German companies as well as government organizations across Latin America and the U.S. Experts previously said parts of SafePay’s code resemble LockBit, a largely defunct ransomware operation that was previously responsible for hundreds of attacks. SafePay has recently taken credit for attacks on one of the U.S.'s biggest providers of IT products and services, British tech company Microlise and government technology contractor Conduent. The SafePay attack on Conduent caused significant damage across the U.S. because of the company’s role in Medicaid, child support, food assistance, roadway tolls and more. Conduent announced a $80 million settlement last Friday in response to a class action lawsuit filed in the wake of the ransomware attack. 1wr3jqv.text: Development platform Zeabur has disclosed details of a cybersecurity incident in which an attacker used leaked internal credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure and steal over 3.2 million environment variable records and information for 321,810 accounts. The attackers used stolen administrator credentials and cloud access keys to compromise Zeabur’s shared hosting infrastructure and dedicated servers, eventually gaining access to its production database. “On October 14–15, 2026, an attacker used leaked Zeabur internal credentials to break into the shared cluster, some Dedicated Servers, and Zeabur internal systems, and eventually read the platform database,” Zeabur’s announcement reads. Attack chainSource: Zeabur Zeabur is a developer hosting and deployment platform that lets developers connect a GitHub repository and have the platform handle deployment, databases, HTTPS, and infrastructure management. In late August 2026, the company suffered another security breach when hackers exploited a flaw in a customer’s NextChat application and then moved through poorly isolated internal systems. This led to the theft of AWS credentials and access to the production database, exposing account information, API keys, and other secrets stored there. In the latest incident, Zeabur says the compromise was broader, affecting shared clusters across nine regions, 321,810 accounts, and roughly 3.2 million environment-variable records. Also, Zeabur confirmed root sign-ins on 101 GCP servers by 92 users, with the attackers adding SSH keys to 50 servers and attaching 16 customer disk copies to their own virtual machines. Data breach scopeSource: Zeabur The company says that attackers likely obtained the credentials they used in the second attack during the August breach, though it hasn’t confirmed this. Beyond failing to store credentials in encrypted form, Zeabur also failed to rotate all administrator account credentials since the August incident, while administrator portals remained accessible to the public internet. “The admin tokens had no expiry, had not been rotated since they were created in January 2024, and were not included in the post-August rotation,” explained Zeabur. Users are urged to rotate exposed credentials and secrets immediately, revoke all active sessions, and rebuild compromised GCP servers. Variables previously migrated exclusively to customers’ own servers as part of the August incident response escaped this latest platform database exposure, although compromised hosts could still expose them. Threat actor's activity and vendor response timesSource: Zeabur Zeabur announces shutdown After discovering the latest security incident, Zeabur announced over the weekend that it will shut down its services starting December 1, 2026, and finish by December 31, 2026. The decision comes after 3.5 years of continuous growth, including a record year in 2026, but Zeabur said scaling the project to meet market demand has made it increasingly complex and difficult to maintain, and the recent security failures reflect that. “After the August incident, we spent a long time discussing and struggling with what to do next,” explained Zeabur. “Following this latest incident, we reassessed what it would take to keep operating and the responsibilities our team could carry. We ultimately decided to wind down.” On December 1, renewals will be disabled, and all running services on shared clusters will be paused. By the end of the year, all dedicated servers will expire and shut down, and all shared clusters will stop. Users may be given additional time for data migration, though no concrete timelines on that front have been provided yet. f62khy.text: A cyberattack on a contractor for California’s Department of Education (CDE) exposed troves of sensitive information covering all children enrolled in public schools over the last three years. The CDE released multiple statements over the last week warning the state’s students that assessment contractor Educational Testing Service (ETS) suffered a months-long data breach. The student information copied by hackers includes: Student names, dates of birth, residential addresses, schools, districts, and grade levels;Statewide Student Identifiers (SSID) and local student identifiers;Gender, race or ethnicity, primary language, country of origin, and English learner status;Disability and Section 504 status, testing accommodations, and primary disability type;Eligibility status for the following programs: Title I, Part A; Title I, Part C; McKinney-Vento; and Military Connected Student; and/orEnglish language proficiency information and statewide assessment registration, participation, and results, where applicable. Those affected include current and former students enrolled in California public schools between 2023 and the current school year, as well as students who left a California school since 2006 and did not confirm transfer to another school with the CDE. CDE hired ETS to provide testing to California K-12 public schools, which enrolled more than 5.7 million students in the 2025 school year. ETS manages the California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) and the English Language Proficiency Assessments for California (ELPAC) exams given each year. ETS, which did not respond to requests for comment, said in a release that hackers copied student information through a secure file transfer protocol site this year from May 22 to September 18. After discovering the breach on September 25, ETS initially disabled the account used to steal the information and eventually took the entire site offline before building an entirely new platform in response to the hack. “After working with law enforcement and cybersecurity experts, ETS has taken steps to reduce the potential risk of the data being made publicly accessible,” CDE said. “Furthermore, ETS, following regular web monitoring, has, to date, not uncovered any evidence that the information has been made public.” A spokesperson for CDE declined to explain what steps ETS took to reduce the risk of the data being made publicly accessible. The ETS statement claims it worked with “law enforcement as well as with cybersecurity experts” to reduce the risk of the incident. No hacking group has said it was responsible for the attack as of Tuesday. The state began notifying families of the incident on October 16 and said it will continue to distribute notices of the attack through November. CDE said it is working with state cybersecurity experts and other agencies to assess how the incident will impact California students. They are also “reviewing… ETS’s compliance with applicable data security and contractual requirements.” ETS said it has “halted normal enrollment data processing and paused certain testing activities while the security of its systems are assessed, and the investigation continues.” CDE explained that it is working to minimize the disruption and resume the affected testing as soon as possible. Educational service providers like ETS have been repeatedly targeted by cybercriminals – with multiple incidents impacting large companies like PowerSchool, Instructure, Illuminate Education, McGraw Hill, Kaplan and more. 1os0fbb.text: A holding company formerly known as 23andMe has agreed to pay California $6 million to resolve allegations that it did not effectively shield customers’ personal and genetic data, enabling a massive 2023 breach that exposed sensitive information belonging to nearly 7 million people. The settlement is pending approval by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in the Eastern District of Missouri and ensures affected consumers maintain the right to delete their data and order genetic samples be destroyed, according to a press release Monday from California Attorney General Rob Bonta. In March 2025, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy and sold customers’ saliva samples and genetic data to the TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit created by 23andMe’s former founder and CEO Anne Wojkicki. In addition to running 23andMe, Wojcicki is the CEO of the Chrome Holding Company, the entity that settled with Bonta. TTAM did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chrome Holding Company does not employ anyone authorized to talk to the press. 23andMe was a longtime Silicon Valley juggernaut, but its fortunes waned over time as the marketplace for people seeking genetic testing shrank.The data breach dealt the final blow. “23andMe collected genetic data about millions of people and failed to meet its obligation to keep that information safe,” Bonta said. “Companies cannot evade California’s consumer protection and privacy laws by filing for bankruptcy.” In July, 23andMe settled with a coalition of 42 additional state attorneys general for $18 million.

6qakht.text: OpenAI confirmed that its newer models are much better at writing and migrating software in older programming languages. The company lists programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic as a few examples where it has seen significant improvements. OpenAI says COBOL supports more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions, and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is still used in areas such as weather forecasting and nuclear reactor safety analysis. "These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world," OpenAI explained in a blog post. To measure progress, OpenAI created MultiLangBench, which asks models to build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 programming languages. GPT-6 Astra reached an average test pass rate of 87.4%, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol. In COBOL specifically, Astra jumped from 10.9% to 72.1%, while Fortran improved from 21.4% to 83.5%. "Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%)," OpenAI noted. GPT-6.1 Sol is much better at migrating COBOL OpenAI also tested whether its models could migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust without changing their behaviour. "GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol's 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost," OpenAI said. "At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation." This work could help companies modernize older software, although production migrations would still require expert review and testing. rvl9v5.text: A hacker who took part in attacks on tax preparation businesses was sentenced to eight years in federal prison and ordered to pay back millions of dollars in damages after pleading guilty to multiple charges. Nigerian national Chukwuemeka Amachukwu was extradited from France last year on fraud, hacking and identity theft charges. Prosecutors accused Amachukwu of leading a group that used spearphishing emails to breach tax preparation businesses dating back to 2019. U.S. District Judge Paul Gardephe gave Amachukwu an eight-year sentence as well as one year of supervised release and an order to pay restitution of more than $3.6 million. “Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into U.S. businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “These crimes imposed significant harm on the victims and the public, and so it is only appropriate that the crimes also come with a significant sentence for the defendant.” Court documents showed Amachukwu worked with Kingsley Uchelue Utulu and other Nigeria-based hackers to break into the tax businesses and steal information on about 800 business customers. They used the stolen information to file fraudulent state and federal tax returns and tried to get about $8.4 million in tax refunds — ultimately succeeding in obtaining $2.5 million. One incident took place in May 2021, when the men sent a phishing email to an employee of a Manhattan-based tax preparation business, infecting the company with malware. Once inside, the men allegedly stole the tax information of the business’ customers and used it to take a number of fraudulent actions. The group also used the information they stole to file claims with the Small Business Administration’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program, earning about $819,000 in fraudulent payouts. Amachukwu and his group conducted several other fraud schemes that allowed them to steal millions. He earned more than $7 million by impersonating wealthy overseas businessmen and offering fake standby letters of credit to U.S. victims. In June, Amachukwu’s co-conspirator Utulu was sentenced to five years in prison for his role in the scheme after being arrested in the U.K. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

xtc7pt.text: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates are compromised, Mozilla and Google's Chrome Root Program confirms on October 20. An intermediate CA signs the certificates that websites present, so anyone holding one of these keys could issue a certificate for any website that a browser would accept. A researcher reported the compromise to the root programs on the evening of October 17, and Chrome and Firefox blocked the eight certificates within hours, after Chrome verified the findings. No TLS certificate chaining to the six intermediates used for websites had been logged to Certificate Transparency (CT) before Chrome's block, so none could have been trusted by default in Chrome or any other browser that requires CT logging, the Chrome Root Program said. It is not known how the keys left eMudhra, when, or whether anyone besides the researcher holds them. The keys are the ones Go blocked in its October 20 security releases without naming the CA, as The Hacker News reported earlier. The eight hash values in Go's code match the eight certificates. Go handled the fix on its URGENT track, which its security policy reserves for threats to the ecosystem's integrity or flaws being exploited in the wild, and neither the issue nor the release notes say which applied. What Was Compromised eMudhra is an Indian CA that sells certificates under the emSign brand through companies in India, the United States, and the Netherlands, and it has roots in the Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple root stores. The eight compromised certificates are: TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, United States) TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C The six TLS certificates were issued by emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, a root in the Chrome and Apple stores and, until October 20, in Mozilla's. Each of the eight also exists as a second certificate with the same public key, cross-signed by Sectigo under its AAA Certificate Services root, according to a certificate list published by Dennis Jackson, a Mozilla cryptography engineer. Chrome did not need to block the two code-signing certificates, because its TLS verifier will not build a path through an intermediate restricted to code signing, the Chrome Root Program said. Who Is Protected, and How The Chrome Root Program received the report at 18:05 UTC on October 17 and had a CRLSet update blocking the six TLS intermediates in place by 19:45 UTC. Mozilla received it at 20:06 UTC and finished pushing a OneCRL block to Firefox installations with standard settings at 22:59 UTC. CRLSets and OneCRL are revocation lists that the two browsers fetch on their own, so neither needed an update or a restart. Chrome's block matches the public key rather than the certificate, so it also catches the Sectigo cross-signed copies. It is the same mechanism Chrome used earlier this month against rogue certificates for Google domains. The researcher, credited by Mozilla only as Wayne, signed the message "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each of the eight keys and sent it to the root programs that day, according to Jackson, who published the signatures and certificates on a one-page site. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates. Apple blocked them on October 19, Microsoft on October 20, and other trust stores were notified on October 19, according to Jackson's site. The cross-signed copies did not widen the risk in Chrome or Firefox. Both stopped trusting Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root for websites in April 2025, and Chrome's root store file does not carry it. Apple's root list for iOS 26 and macOS 26, published in December 2025, includes it. Mozilla does not believe, for now, that the problem affects other CAs, Jackson wrote on Mozilla's policy list, and Chrome said it checked every other CA certificate in its store and "found no other instances of this failure mode." What to Update Browsers get revocation pushed to them. Many other programs that check TLS certificates, from Go binaries to anything using Python's certifi bundle, do not check revocation data and keep trusting a chain until their code or their root bundle changes. Mozilla's advice to anyone who runs a trust store: nothing is needed where clients reliably check revocation and refuse connections when they cannot check, the eight intermediates should be blocked now where the software can block individual intermediates; and otherwise the operator should consider removing trust in the roots that signed them. The fixes published so far, and what each one does: add border: Software Fixed in What it does Status Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 Rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys (CVE-2026-111943) Released October 20, rebuild required Firefox 158.0.1 , ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 Carries the OneCRL block for installations that cannot receive Remote Settings ( CVE-2026-113470 ) Released October 20 NSS 3.131.1 Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the trusted list Released October 20 Python certifi 2026.10.19 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the bundle Released Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Released Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 Excludes emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services by public key Released Node.js None yet A draft change would block the eight keys Pending Composer ca-bundle None yet An open change would remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Pending Go's filter sits in the standard library and rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys, on Go's own verifier and on the macOS and Windows system-verifier paths, and the change adds no setting to turn it off. A program picks it up only when rebuilt with the new release; Go 1.25 and older are out of support and get no fixes. Three of the fixes work by removing roots rather than blocking the keys. certifi, webpki-roots, and Homebrew's ca-certificates drop emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their bundles, and Homebrew also drops Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root and emSign Root TLS CA - G3. That also cuts off every legitimate certificate that chains to those roots. Mozilla, which made the same change to NSS, said some servers will become unavailable to non-Firefox users of its trust list until those servers move to new certificate chains. Firefox needs nothing unless Remote Settings is disabled by policy or blocked on the network. The October 20 releases carry the block list for those installations. None of the sources provide a way to detect past misuse of the keys beyond Chrome's CT search, which covers only logged certificates. What Happens to eMudhra Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from NSS on October 20. Chrome will remove the same root in version 43 of its root store and is reviewing the status of eMudhra's other root in its store, emSign Root CA - G1, the Chrome Root Program said, citing the seriousness of the incident. How the keys left eMudhra and when remain open questions. Mozilla said it is working with the CA, other root programs and downstream trust stores on the root cause and will post more when it can. eMudhra's trust-services repository carried no notice about the incident as of October 20. Go has not named the CA on its issue, where its release notes cite "specific security concerns around their operation", and a commenter asked for the hashes in the patch to be explained. Filippo Valsorda, who maintains the cryptography packages in Go's standard library, replied that the keys are compromised and the certificates revoked, that Linux root stores are too poorly maintained for revocation to reach applications, and that putting the keys in code is the only option for now.

1rlr7pt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Cybersecurity researchers have released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a recently patched critical security flaw impacting Fortinet FortiSIEM that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-106173 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a critical path traversal flaw that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via specially crafted packets. Patches for the flaw were released last week by Fortinet in the following versions - FortiSIEM 7.5.0 (Upgrade to 7.5.1 or above) FortiSIEM 7.6 (Not affected) According to Horizon3.ai, the issue involves an unauthenticated attacker connecting to the gRPC service listening on TCP port 27918 and exploiting the flaw to overwrite an existing file outside of the intended directory and turn the arbitrary-file-write primitive into remote code execution. "The FortiSIEM gRPC QueryResultReq handler processes untrusted metadata without proper path validation," Horizon3.ai said. "By crafting metadata containing both path traversal sequences (../) and NUL-byte injection within gRPC's HTTP/2 and HPACK encoding layers, an attacker can write arbitrary files to the file system." The problem stems from a case of unsafe path construction within a function named SendQueryResult(), which passes a user-supplied "query-id" parameter directly without sufficient validation. In other words, an attacker can leverage this flaw to include directory traversal sequences such as "../" and escape that directory. However, this only allows an attacker to navigate to a directory of their choice and write to it, but not to opt for a file name because the program automatically adds its own file name "result-<source IP address>-0-0-<id>.dat," where <id> is a counter value controlled by the server. That's where a second weakness enters the picture: a null byte ("\0") can be embedded in the "query-id" parameter, causing the operating system to interpret it as a string terminator and discard everything that comes after it. This, in turn, results in the appended file name suffix being ignored when the path is passed to the file-opening function. An attacker could exploit this behavior to craft a "query-id" value with "\0" placed such that it's preceded by the actual file name to be overwritten – i.e., "../../../../../opt/charting/redishb.sh\0..." The file in question is a shell script that performs health checks on the Redis service and is run every 60 seconds by a cron job. "The write lands on the exact path that preceded the null byte," Zach Hanley, Chief Attack Engineer at Horizon3.ai, said. "Pointed at an existing file, this overwrites it in place, keeping the original owner and permissions; a second variant uses two requests to create a brand-new file with an exact name."

d57pzn.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks has disclosed that it's continuing to observe exploitation of a now-patched security flaw impacting PAN-OS and Prisma Access by ransomware actors. The activity relates to CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw that could be exploited by bad actors to set up unauthorized VPN connections. It was patched by Palo Alto Networks in May 2026 and was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CSIA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026. "Ransomware operators exploiting CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka INC)," Unit 42 researchers said in an update shared on Monday. The development comes days after ReliaQuest said it detected both Qilin and Settra ransomware groups actively exploiting the flaw in financially-motivated attacks. According to Unit 42, the threat actors are weaponizing the flaw to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, and then bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Upon setting up a VPN session, the attackers have been found to engage in the following post-compromise activity - Conduct internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools. Move laterally across the network via RDP and SMB. Stage additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment. Attacks mounted by these groups are said to have targeted a wide range of sectors, including education, financial services, healthcare, high technology, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and retail. "The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer," Unit 42 said. "In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK)." This approach, the network security vendor added, circumvents in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security protections, allowing the threat actors to obtain domain-wide credentials. Attackers have also been observed chaining the initial access method with other exploit tools, including efforts to target Veeam backup infrastructure by abusing known flaws (CVE-2023-27532) to inflict maximum damage. It's worth noting that Qilin's exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 was previously flagged by Arctic Wolf in July 2026, with attacks ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion. Besides applying the latest fixes, Palo Alto Networks is recommending that organizations proactively hunt for indicators of compromise and initiate appropriate incident response protocols if successful gateway-connected events are detected.

7ji5s8.text: The European Union’s new cyber rules require manufacturers to report attacks exploiting their end-of-life products, but does not force them to fix the issues, the bloc’s cybersecurity agency said Monday, after a cyberattack hit hundreds of French supermarkets’ refrigeration systems. Earlier this month, hackers compromised internet-exposed remote controllers for refrigeration systems at numerous French supermarkets, forcing some units into a continuous defrost cycle at 50°C, according to reports at the time. Grocery chains including Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix, Leclerc and Coopérative U were affected, with monetary losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros as spoiled food stock had to be thrown away. France’s cybersecurity agency ANSSI said it was “aware of the compromise of refrigeration system remote controllers,” naming Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC series, Copeland’s xweb and Dixell’s xweb products. The agency’s emergency response team, CERT-FR, issued an alert last Monday and ANSSI urged operators to disconnect or filter any controllers exposed to the internet to prevent further attacks. “Investigations are on-going,” the agency told Recorded Future News, adding that it was coordinating preventive and remediation measures across sectors that might be affected, “with a specific focus on mass retailers.” In a statement, Copeland acknowledged “the vulnerability identified in a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers,” adding it was “currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk.” The company said it would “continue to support customers in strengthening cybersecurity through supported products, current software and industry-recommended practices.” It did not say how many customers were affected. Danfoss did not respond to a request for comment, but has said its affected units were also end-of-life. The Paris prosecutor’s office told Recorded Future News it had received “about ten complaints” and estimated the “number of victims at around 700.” Its investigation is also ongoing, and it said that to date no perpetrator has claimed responsibility for the attack. EU response Provisions of the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act that took effect last month require manufacturers of connected hardware and software devices sold in the bloc — from consumer gadgets to industrial controllers like those hit in France — to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting their products. ENISA — the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity — told Recorded Future News that the obligation covers end-of-life products “no longer sold in the EU, but which remain in use,” and that “the reporting obligations continue to apply after a product with digital elements is no longer supported.” However the law’s separate obligations to handle vulnerabilities, including fixing them and issuing free security updates, apply only during a product’s support period, which manufacturers define. Where a product was placed on the market before December 11, 2027, or its support has ended — as in the fridge controllers targeted in this instance — “the manufacturer is not required to comply with the vulnerability handling obligations,” said ENISA. The agency declined to share information on specific notices it may have received from manufacturers and would not say whether any had reported the attacks. It said the EU CSIRTs Network of national cyber emergency response teams “is actively exchanging info and monitoring the situation.” ANSSI added it was also “equally mobilized at the European level and is maintaining regular dialogue with its counterparts.” No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

wdh6gf.text: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is ordering federal civilian agencies to stop using DeepSeek products and remove them from government systems. The order also covers products from the Chinese AI company's affiliates and third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology. DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd) develops large language models and offers a chatbot, API services, and models suitable for coding and reasoning tasks. Its AI tools became extremely popular early on, but were but were soon followed by reports of security risks [1, 2, 3, 4] and concerns about the potential for Chinese authorities to access users’ conversations. The DHS is now taking regulatory action to limit the use of DeepSeek and derivatives on critical systems in the United States, and has issued a notice of order for agencies to: Immediately exclude covered products from procurement, including approved-product lists and purchasing marketplaces. Immediately remove covered products from agency IT systems, or seek an exception. Submit any exception requests within 60 days of the order’s issuance, explaining the justification and proposed risk mitigations. CISA will review requests and issue written approvals or denials. The order applies to federal civilian agencies within DHS’s authority and is not a general ban on private or consumer use. DHS explained that the order stems from concerns about the Chinese government accessing DeepSeek infrastructure, collecting personal information and tracking users, and potentially transferring sensitive government data to China. The document also raises concerns about potential malware in DeepSeek models, citing a February 2025 report from NowSecure that identified security vulnerabilities in the DeepSeek iOS app. NowSecure examined the app and found unencrypted data transmissions, weak encryption algorithms, insecure local storage, user fingerprinting risks, and data sharing with ByteDance, the Chinese tech giant behind the TikTok short-form video platform. The order was published in the Federal Register earlier today, a day after appearing on Public Inspection. Executive agencies can request exceptions within 60 days of the issuance date of the order. For agencies that cannot comply with this order because of internal capability restrictions, CISA will provide the necessary technical assistance. 1r9tgcc.text: A Chinese-speaking criminal pointed autonomous AI agents at company websites and let them break in with almost no help, and a security researcher watched it happen because the operators left their control panels open on the internet. The agents tried more than 1,200 sites and reached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm-equipment maker Deere, appliance company SharkNinja and engine maker Cummins, according to Reuters, which reviewed the attacker's own records to identify them. How much data, if any, was taken is not known. The researcher, Snorre Fagerland of the security firm NorForge, found the operations by scanning the internet for exposed copies of Cairn, an open-source AI tool popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, he found about two dozen Cairn instances being used maliciously, which let him read the attackers' work in real time. He set out the findings on Monday, and Reuters, which saw the report before publication, named the victims from its own review of the attacker's activity. Cairn gives AI agents a starting point and a goal, then lets them work toward it step by step. The agents post what they find to a shared board, and the human operator can add hints along the way. It was built for authorized penetration testing and does other jobs too, but here it was pointed at online shops without permission. Cairn's author, who posts as "le1xia0," told Reuters the tool was not designed for hacking attacks and that harmful use was not their intention. What the agents did, and who was hit NorForge grouped the exposed panels into three clusters and judged more than 20 of them likely to be malicious. The busiest cluster, which NorForge calls AIA0001, is Chinese-language and links 14 panels to more than 1,100 attack projects. Its aim seems to be lasting access to shop and payment systems for later use, NorForge said, with targets in the United States, Japan and Australia. A typical task told the agents to find a way to run code on a shop and then plant a web shell uploader. That is a form that saves uploaded files, not one that runs commands, and attackers can swap it for something worse at any time. NorForge checked one claimed break-in, at a large hardware-parts vendor, and found the web shell live. It independently confirmed the compromise of one very large US retailer, in which the agents found the single cookie setting that selected a vulnerable backend server. The three named companies told Reuters the damage was limited. Deere said it took steps to fix the problem and had no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product-support site and that it had contained the threat. Cummins said it was investigating a report of a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors. Two smaller businesses also told Reuters they were compromised. One documented intrusion, by the agent's own account, worked through unauthorized write access to a memcached session store, unsafe handling of saved PHP objects, and a weakness in old Zend Framework code. The paths differ from victim to victim, so this is one chain, not a single method. Cheap, fast, and largely unsupervised The instructions were short. The Chinese-speaking operator sketched out preferred tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, Reuters reported, and the agents went from there. Successful break-ins took a little under 23 hours on average, NorForge found, and the overall success rate across the tools it saw was around 10%, though it cautioned the clusters chase different goals and are not directly comparable. The cost was low, but the figures are rough. NorForge put the average at about $5 a task, counting attempts that failed or ended early, and said the uncertainty is considerable. Fagerland separately told Reuters the whole campaign had used about $5,000 worth of tokens, or roughly $50 per successful hack. All the AIA0001 tasks ran under a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash, which could point to a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model driven by Anthropic's Claude Code. Neither the researcher nor Reuters confirmed the models, and Reuters said only that the campaign appeared to use DeepSeek and Claude Code. The open panels leak the victims' secrets too Leaving a Cairn panel open is a separate problem from the break-ins. The panels show who is being attacked, what weaknesses were found, and which credentials and keys were taken, so having your site tested on an open instance can expose your secrets, whatever the test's outcome. NorForge ran the secrets scanner Trufflehog over the panel data and found hundreds of secrets, 11% of which it verified as still valid. The panels also appear to expose the full set of the tool's controls, including the ability to start and stop projects, feed in new data, and point agents to different targets. NorForge said it did not test whether those controls work without a login. A second, English-language cluster went further and exposed the operators' own SSH logins to their staging servers; NorForge said it did not log in. The exposure is not only a criminal problem. NorForge also found apparently legitimate penetration-testing firms that had left real client tests on unsecured panels, putting their customers' data at the same risk. What to check, and where this came from Defenders can act on a few points: Exposed panels. Agent control panels of this kind often answer on port 8000, so an exposed one without a login is worth hunting for. Stray upload forms. An unexpected file-upload form sitting in a hidden directory is the foothold these agents aimed for. Magento patching. A worker directory NorForge browsed held a proof-of-concept for a critical Magento flaw, StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), and a test lab for it. There is no evidence it was used in these break-ins, but any shop still on an affected build should apply Adobe's hotfix for it: Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9, or Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9. NorForge's search followed a September report by Gambit Security, a separate campaign in which a criminal used Cairn alongside two other AI tools to steal credit cards; that report is what first flagged Cairn on an attacker's server. No source links the two operations. NorForge said it is working with Reuters to warn victims and is asking hosting firms to take the panels down, an effort it said depends on how the hosts respond.

1dzr1ii.text: For agencies responsible for protecting Criminal Justice Information (CJI), meeting CJIS requirements means more than putting security controls in place. Those controls need to work across the systems staff use every day, and agencies need to be able to prove they're effective. But, between legacy systems, stretched IT teams, and constantly changing access needs, even agencies with strong security practices can struggle to apply controls consistently and keep the evidence auditors expect. So, where should you focus your efforts? In this article, we'll walk through five key areas agencies should be paying attention to under CJIS v6.1, with practical advice to make compliance easier to manage. Multi-Factor Authentication CJIS v6.1 requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged accounts under controls IA-2(1) and IA-2(2), covering local, network, and remote access. The challenge is making sure no accounts slip through the cracks. Start by reviewing MFA coverage across your environment, paying particular attention to legacy applications and administrative accounts. When implementing MFA, consider phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys. You'll also need reliable processes for enrolling, replacing, and revoking authenticators. Solutions like Specops Secure Access help agencies comply by extending MFA protection to Windows logons, RDP, RADIUS, and offline access, with flexible options including authenticator apps and YubiKeys. Its event API integrations also help provide evidence for compliance audits. Remember, MFA isn't a one-time fix. Revisit your configurations as systems and access needs change. Account Management and Privileges Access permissions can quickly become outdated as employees change roles or leave, a risk which CJIS v6.1 aims to reduce by enforcing effective account management and least privilege. Start by keeping an accurate inventory of user, administrative, service, and temporary accounts. Limit permissions to what is needed for each role, separate administrative privileges from everyday activities, and automate account provisioning and removal where possible. Review accounts and privileges at least annually. Temporary and emergency accounts must be removed within 72 hours, while accounts inactive for 90 days must be disabled within one week. The key is making access reviews an ongoing process, not just an annual exercise. Passwords IA-5 sets an eight-character password minimum and is a Priority 1 control, so has been sanctionable since October 2024. Aligning with NIST recommendations, agencies should encourage longer, unique passphrases and use approved password managers to reduce reuse. Agencies should also: Screen for compromised passwords, updating password blocklists at least quarterly and whenever compromise is suspected. Block weak or reused passwords during creation or reset. Limit failed login attempts to no more than five per account. This is where Specops Password Policy can help. It simplifies password policy management across Active Directory, continuously checking against over 6 billion compromised passwords and scanning daily for newly exposed credentials. Customizable grace periods help reduce unnecessary lockouts when a compromised password is found, while compliance templates and reporting make it easier to track your progress. Finally, check annual password change requirements with your CJIS Systems Agency, as IA-5 still specifies a yearly change or refresh despite guidance discouraging unnecessary resets. Logging Audit logs help agencies detect suspicious activity and investigate security incidents. However, collecting logs isn't enough. Agencies also need to capture the right events, review records regularly, and protect them against tampering. Start by checking logging coverage across systems handling CJI. Make sure records capture who did what and when, as well as the outcome. Centralizing logs in a SIEM can make suspicious activity easier to spot. Audit Readiness Agencies are audited at least once every three years, but you’re expected to maintain compliance between audits. Rather than scrambling to pull evidence together at the last minute, it’s better to treat CJIS compliance as an ongoing responsibility. Some best practices include: Maintaining an inventory of applicable security controls and identifying who is responsible for implementing, reviewing, and documenting each one. Keeping evidence organized, including records of MFA configurations, access reviews, audit logs, security policies, training, and assessment results. That makes it easier to demonstrate compliance. Documenting identified weaknesses and setting deadlines for resolving them. In line with CA-5, you should update remediation plans at least every six months or when new information becomes available. Conducting internal assessments to identify issues before a formal assessment. Building security monitoring and compliance reviews into everyday IT operations, so changes or new risks don't go unnoticed. By making audit preparation part of routine security management, agencies can identify gaps earlier, reduce the work involved in formal assessments, and maintain a stronger compliance posture between audits. Strengthen Your CJIS Compliance Posture CJIS compliance isn't a one-and-done exercise. As systems and security risks change, agencies need to make sure their controls keep pace. By regularly reviewing controls and keeping evidence organized, you can make compliance easier to manage while strengthening your agency's security. Passwords are a good place to start when assessing your CJIS compliance. But how do you know where the gaps are? Specops Password Auditor offers a free, read-only Active Directory scan that highlights password policy gaps against CJIS requirements and flags risks, including compromised passwords. It’s a quick way to see where you currently stand and what needs attention. If you’re looking to simplify meeting CJIS password and MFA requirements, book a demo with Specops and see how we can help your agency strengthen security and maintain compliance. 9snxkl.text: A Nigerian national was sentenced to eight years in prison for his involvement in a series of spearphishing attacks targeting US tax preparation businesses since 2019. 40-year-old Chukwuemeka Victor Amachukwu (also known as Chukwuemeka Victor Eletuo and So Kwan Leung) has pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit computer intrusions and wire fraud after being extradited from France to the United States in August 2025. "Chukwuemeka Amachukwu believed he was operating safely offshore when he targeted his victims, but he has now been held to account and now faces a serious sentence for his crimes," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald in a Monday press release. "Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into US businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud. These crimes imposed significant harm on the victims and the public, and so it is only appropriate that the crimes also come with a significant sentence for the defendant." According to court documents, Amachukwu and his accomplices stole more than $3 million after filing fraudulent tax and loan applications with the Internal Revenue Service and state tax authorities using their victims' stolen personal data. Together with co-defendant Kingsley Uchelue Utulu and other Nigerian co-conspirators, Amachukwu launched spearphishing attacks against tax preparation businesses in New York, Texas, and other US states between 2019 and 2021, gaining unauthorized access to their targets' computers and stealing the tax and personally identifiable information (PII) of at least 800 customers. In total, he allegedly obtained about $2.5 million in fraudulent tax refunds (after filing for $8.4 million in refunds) and another $819,000 through fraudulent loan applications with the Small Business Administration's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program. Amachukwu was also involved in a fake investment scheme that offered potential US victims investments in what the scammers described as valuable standby letters of credit. However, these investments did not exist, and the fraudsters stole more than $7 million from multiple victims. In addition to the prison term, the court sentenced Amachukwu to one year of supervised release and ordered him to pay $3.6 million in restitution and forfeit nearly $11 million. 1hrqxla.text: The iPhone of Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade and a prominent supporter of Serbia's student protest movement, was infected with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware in 2026, the Citizen Lab said on October 19. The finding came six days before Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary election. The infection used a zero-click exploit, meaning Đokić did not have to tap a link or open a file for it to work. The lab found the infection with high confidence, but its note provides no date within 2026, does not identify who was behind the attack, and notes that its investigation is ongoing. The election was called in September after nearly two years of protests that began when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, analyzed forensic artifacts from the phone at Đokić's request, working with the Serbian digital-rights group SHARE Foundation. SHARE led the investigation of an earlier wave of Serbian cases made public in September. A second case concerns Rade Bajić, a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia's Public Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime who worked on the "Generalštab" corruption investigation into a Kushner-linked property project in Belgrade. Bajić received an Apple Threat Notification on August 13 and a reminder on August 27. Apple sends these alerts when it detects activity consistent with an attack by mercenary spyware, the commercial hacking tools that companies such as NSO sell to governments, and it does not say who is behind the attacks. The Citizen Lab treats a notification as a high-confidence sign that Bajić's phone was likely targeted. Its forensic analysis of the device is ongoing, and the note does not say whether the phone was infected. The Generalštab case concerns the removal of heritage protection from Belgrade's bombed-out former army General Staff complex to clear the way for a luxury development backed by a company linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law. In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials with abuse of office and falsifying documents in the case, the Associated Press reported. Bajić says he was taken off the investigation in November 2025 without explanation, and in February he spoke about the case at a protest called by student activists outside Serbia's Constitutional Court. The lab's note does not say what, if anything, was taken from the rector's phone. Pegasus gives whoever operates it the same access as the phone's owner, including private and encrypted messages, and can switch on the microphone and camera without the owner knowing, according to the lab's analysis of the September case. Đokić called the spyware on his phone "another attempt of intimidation" in an English-language statement published by the university, and demanded an independent investigation without delay, with its results made public and whoever installed and used the spyware prosecuted. Police raided the rector's offices on March 31 and seized computers and servers, he said at the time. The Security Information Agency (BIA), Serbia's civilian security service, dismissed the September allegations that students and opposition politicians had been spied on as "purely trivial sensationalism" in a statement on September 3, as translated by the broadcaster N1, and said it operates strictly within Serbian law. The two cases extend a wave that SHARE reported on September 2, when it said at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists, an opposition MP and a local councilor, had been targeted with spyware since the start of the year. Twelve of them had received Apple Threat Notifications in August, the month Apple warned users in 110 countries. One was Jelena Kontić, a student whose Pegasus infection the Citizen Lab confirmed. The other two had a new version of NoviSpy, an Android spyware, installed on their phones. By the Citizen Lab's count, the two new cases bring the number of people in Serbian civil society publicly known to have been targeted or infected with mercenary spyware this year to at least 16. Amnesty International reported in December 2024 that NoviSpy was configured to send stolen data to a server whose IP address belonged to the BIA and was installed on activists' and journalists' phones during police questioning, after the devices were unlocked with Cellebrite forensic tools. Lawyers for Kontić filed a criminal complaint on October 6 against unidentified individuals in the BIA and the police, as well as people responsible at NSO Group. Pegasus is sold only to governments and state agencies, SHARE says, and the complaints already filed over spyware in Serbia have brought no effective action. The note does not name the flaw used against Đokić's phone or say whether current iOS releases block it, so there is no case-specific fix to install. The lab's advice for people at risk because of who they are or what they do: Turn on Lockdown Mode on your iPhone and keep iOS up to date. If you receive an Apple Threat Notification, assume the phone is infected until an expert has checked it, and get help at once: SHARE Foundation in Serbia, or Access Now's Digital Security Helpline elsewhere. Have close contacts, such as family members and people they work with, screened for spyware too.

1fso7sv.text: Microsoft announced that IT administrators can now use quick machine recovery on Windows Server 2025 after installing the October 2026 security update. Quick machine recovery (QMR) lets IT admins fix critical boot failures with targeted Windows Update fixes without physical access to affected systems. When enabled, it boots into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) and launches the QMR Tool if Windows 11 fails to start because of a configuration change or a new driver. It then sends crash data to Microsoft, which can remotely fix issues by adjusting settings or removing problematic drivers or updates. "With the October 2026 security update, quick machine recovery extends to Windows Server 2025," the company said in a message center update. "Quick machine recovery is designed to help restore devices experiencing widespread boot issues by using the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to search Windows Update for applicable remediations." On Windows Server 2025, cloud remediation is disabled by default, but admins can enable it via Group Policy under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Quick Machine Recovery to retrieve and apply cloud-sourced remediation. For local configuration, admins must sign in to the target server with administrator permissions and use the Local Group Policy Editor. In domain configurations, they can use Group Policy Management on a Windows Server or an administration computer, but they also need permissions to edit the GPO and link it to the intended organizational unit (OU). To disable QMR through Group Policy, admins have to explicitly turn off 'Enable Cloud Remediation' to prevent cloud-sourced remediation and disable 'Enable Auto Remediation' to block automatic application of local remediation packages. This can be done by going through the following steps: Open the local policy or domain GPO that manages the target Windows Server 2025 computers. Go to Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Quick Machine Recovery. Open Enable Cloud Remediation, select Disabled, and select Apply, then OK. Open Enable Auto Remediation, select Disabled, and select Apply, then OK. (Optional) Verify the effective configuration. Microsoft introduced quick machine recovery in November 2024 as part of its Windows Resiliency Initiative at Ignite 2024, in response to a July 2024 outage caused by a buggy CrowdStrike Falcon update that rendered millions of Windows devices unbootable. It began testing in late March 2025, rolling it out to Windows Insiders in the Beta Channel. In November, it also began testing a faster version that now runs a single scan to fix systems with boot problems, rather than looping through solutions.
