1n6mn6v.text: WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden instructions for its support chatbot that told it not to recommend a data protection authority or regulator to users who could no longer delete their accounts, even though WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe tells users they can complain to one. The text sat in the pages' code, never shown on screen, until it was removed by October 18. Whether the chatbot ever followed the instructions is not known: Redact, the data-deletion software company that found the text, read the instructions, not the chatbot's answers. WhatsApp told WIRED the instructions were for the chatbot that users reach by messaging WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they appeared in the pages because of a bug, now fixed. A second block of hidden text on the page about reporting and blocking told the chatbot that once a user mentioned a lawyer, a lawsuit, or a court, it should not cite privacy laws such as the GDPR, even when the user raised them. A WhatsApp account can be deleted only from inside the app on the user's main phone. A user who has lost the phone or the number cannot do it, and the help page on deleting an account says so in a visible note: a deactivated account is deleted 30 days after deactivation, and an inactive one is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days in the US. Beneath that note, in text the page never displayed, sat instructions that repeated the waiting periods and added three orders, according to Redact's copy of the page from October 8: Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number. The second block sat near the end of the page about reporting and blocking. It applied, in its own words, "When a user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation", and from then on told the chatbot not to cite WhatsApp's Terms of Service or Privacy Policy, not to discuss WhatsApp's liability, to send users with legal matters to "a qualified legal professional", and: Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly. On the regulator, WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, effective July 2, 2026, says the opposite. "You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp's lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority," it says. On deletion, the gap is narrower: the hidden text told the chatbot not to suggest that WhatsApp could delete a user's account, while the policy says users "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of" their information. Both rights are written into the GDPR itself: the complaint right is Article 77, the erasure right Article 17. Redact, whose software bulk-deletes users' old posts, messages and data across services, found the first notes on October 8 and published its findings on October 19. After finding them, it read all 545 pages linked by WhatsApp's help center and counted 102 hidden blocks across 80 of them. Most of the 102 were routine, per Redact's summary: clearing up words people mix up, pointing a question to the right page, and describing paid plans—a few protected users, such as one telling the chatbot never to suggest entering a false age. A few were in the same family as the two above. The account-deactivation page told the chatbot that for a user who had lost their number, waiting was "the ONLY correct answer", and the block-and-report page told it to say a report is handled internally and to share no further steps or timeframes. One block named WhatsApp's support chatbot. Redact also checked 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages, which run on the same system, and found no notes like these. The blocks sat in the pages' HTML under the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude and were not shown on screen, so anyone who viewed the page source could read them. WhatsApp's server sent them, with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers, Redact found. Requests Redact sent on October 9 under the user-agent names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and Perplexity's crawlers use came back without the article or the notes. Redact did not test whether any AI assistant acted on them. Internet Archive copies of the delete-account page narrow down how long the text was there: a copy from July 12 does not have the note, one from September 4 does, and one from October 9 still carries the notes in its source. Both notes were still on the live pages at 21:40 UTC on October 15. By 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were removed from all 80 pages, with the pages themselves still up; an archive copy from 02:37 UTC that day shows the change. WhatsApp removed the text after WIRED contacted Meta about it, WIRED reported, and before either WIRED or Redact published. "These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI," WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told WIRED. The company wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice," he said. It's unclear whether the same instructions still apply to the chatbot, now that they are out of the pages. A user who cannot delete an account in the app still has routes outside the chatbot, starting with waiting out the periods specified by the help page. Under WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, a user can always ask WhatsApp to erase their information. In the EU, a user who is not satisfied can complain to their national data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which WhatsApp's policy names and asks people to raise the matter with the organization first, then through its online form.

1tjgbpg.text: A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine. Across the same organization, employees are building useful apps, agents, and automations faster than existing processes can support them. If you work in security, that success introduces a new set of questions. Whose credentials does the workflow use? Which records can it access? Who can see its output? If it starts exposing information it shouldn’t, can you trace what happened and stop further access? Wild code takes root when useful builds spread faster than the processes for owning, securing, and maintaining them. It isn’t simply another name for unapproved software. Employees are creating new capabilities, not just adopting existing products. A small experiment can become an operational dependency before security knows it exists. The risk goes beyond vulnerabilities in generated code. Even code that works as intended can operate with too much access or expose data to the wrong audience: Excessive permissions. A workflow needs a small set of records but runs with credentials that can read or modify far more. Sensitive data exposure. An employee connects an agent to information it doesn’t need, or makes its output available too broadly. Sensitive information can also end up in model requests or logs. Unintended actions. An agent can change records or permissions without an approval boundary appropriate to the action. Orphaned access. A useful workflow keeps running after its creator changes roles or leaves, with no clear owner reviewing its permissions. Investigation gaps. When something goes wrong, security can’t readily establish which identity ran the workflow, what it accessed, or what changed. Employee education, sandboxes, and AI steering committees are a good start, but they aren’t enough to control wild code on their own. A more sustainable approach builds controls into the environment itself: what employees can connect to, what their apps and agents can do, and how that work is monitored once it’s running. Why the usual fixes fall short Education, sandboxes, and steering committees all have a role. The mistake is expecting them to govern software they may never encounter, or control what happens after it starts running. A policy describes what should happen. Security also needs controls that constrain what can happen, evidence of what did happen, and a way to intervene. 1. Education explains good practice, but can’t enforce it An AI policy can explain what’s allowed. Training can introduce good practices. Neither guarantees that someone building a reporting workflow will recognize the moment they cross into handling sensitive data or operating production software. As AI brings more employees into building software, organizations have an opportunity to make practices like least privilege, secrets management, and separating test environments from production more accessible. Policies can set expectations, but employees also need practical guidance and built-in safeguards to apply them in everyday work. Even employees who recognize a risk still face deadlines and pressure to move faster. If the approved route is slow or confusing, knowing the rules doesn’t make following them easier. Education helps people make better decisions. It shouldn’t be the only thing preventing an unsafe connection or an unauthorized action. 2. Sandboxes protect experiments, not their entire future An isolated environment is useful for testing prompts, models, and generated code. But a prototype’s value often depends on eventually reaching real business systems and data. Once a prototype connects to live business systems, it needs controls that extend beyond the test environment. Permissions, monitoring, and change reviews have to remain in place throughout its working life, not just during the experiment. A successful test doesn’t establish which data the production workflow should access or which actions it should be allowed to take. As Brad Rumph, field CTO at Tines, puts it: “Sandboxes solve the design problem and leave the runtime problem alone.” A successful experiment still needs a governed path into operation. Without that path, isolation postpones the hard questions rather than resolving them. 3. Committees can’t review what they can’t see Steering committees can set direction, establish accountability, and make decisions about high-risk use cases. But their review cycles don’t always match the speed at which employees can create and deploy software. A committee might prohibit one risky practice while employees discover another way to achieve the same result. Oversight can also concentrate on engineering, where established controls already exist, while overlooking builds in finance, HR, or operations. The limitation isn’t the quality of the committee. It’s a model that depends on each build becoming visible before it becomes useful. An approval process can’t be the only way security discovers new paths to sensitive data and privileged actions. Put security controls where the work happens The alternative is to build controls into the environment employees use to create, run, and maintain their work. Rather than asking everyone to independently assemble a secure operating model, security teams define shared boundaries with IT and system owners, apply them consistently throughout the lifecycle, and update them as business needs and risks change. Three principles make this practical. 1. Govern before deployment, and keep governing afterward Define permitted data sources, actions, and access before employees connect business systems. Keep those controls in place when the workflow goes live. Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control. Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it. 2. Make the approved route the easiest route Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly. That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs. If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions. AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data. 3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do. Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs. Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations. What this looks like in practice A governed environment should make important security questions answerable without a separate investigation: Accountable ownership. Who owns the workflow, and which identity does it run as? Controlled access. What can it read, change, and send elsewhere? Which actions require approval, and where is that enforced? Protected execution. Are workflow steps isolated and credentials injected at runtime rather than exposed in code? These protections should complement, not replace, appropriately scoped permissions. Traceable activity. Can security establish what ran, what it accessed, and what changed? Clear intervention. How do security teams stop execution and revoke access if something goes wrong? These controls don’t eliminate every risk. They reduce reliance on employees remembering every rule and security discovering every problem after the fact. Keep control as more people build Employees will keep finding valuable ways to build with AI. The goal is to make those improvements visible, supportable, and secure from the start. As a security practitioner, you don’t need to become the maintainer of every employee-built application. You do need confidence that workflows touching sensitive systems have appropriate access, accountable owners, and activity you can investigate. Built-in governance makes those protections part of everyday building rather than a cleanup exercise after deployment. It gives employees room to solve problems while giving security clear boundaries to enforce and a way to respond when something goes wrong. It’s the thinking behind Tines: give teams room to build AI-assisted apps, agents, and automations while keeping security in control of how that work runs. For a closer look at the framework and a readiness checklist, download Taming wild code: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl.

17jp5zp.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 20, 2026Encryption / Software Security Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10, released on October 20, make Go's certificate verifier reject any certificate chain that passes through one of eight intermediate certificate authority keys. Programs built on the new release will refuse connections to sites and services whose certificates were issued under those keys. The Go team says the keys belong to one certificate authority it has not named, and that it is blocking them because of "specific security concerns around their operation." It handled the fix on its URGENT track, the one reserved for its most serious issues, and recommends upgrading immediately. Two days earlier, on October 17, Mozilla added six intermediate certificates issued by eMudhra's emSign Root TLS CA - G3 to OneCRL, the list Firefox uses to block certificates. The Mozilla bug behind those entries is closed to the public, and neither Mozilla nor Go has said what prompted its action. Whether Chrome, Apple, or Microsoft have taken similar action is not established. Go's change lists only the SHA-256 hashes of the eight keys. A commenter on the Go issue matched all eight to eMudhra intermediates by looking the hashes up in certificate records. By that matching, six are TLS intermediates issued under the same emSign Root TLS CA - G3 that Mozilla's entries name, and two are code-signing intermediates under emSign Root CS CA - G3: TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, U.S.) TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C The Hacker News has not independently checked the hashes against the certificates. Mozilla's six entries carry the same issuing root, but Mozilla's records do not name the six certificates. The filter runs whenever a Go program verifies a certificate chain. It hashes each certificate's public key rather than the certificate itself, so a cross-signed copy of one of the eight keys, the same key signed by a different root, is caught as well. It is applied in Go's own verifier and in the macOS and Windows code paths that hand verification to the operating system. A rejected chain returns the error x509: no valid chains built. The change contains no setting to turn the filter off. Given the structure of the code, it also applies when a program supplies its own set of trusted roots, so a private deployment that intentionally trusts one of the eight keys will fail too. The Go team has not said whether that is intended. Go's verifier "doesn't do any revocation checking," as its documentation warns. It also does not read the block lists browsers use, such as the CRLSets Chrome used against rogue Google certificates this month. Blocking a key therefore means shipping it in a release, and programs keep the old behavior until they are rebuilt. Projects including Bluesky's indigo were rebuilt on the new releases on October 20. What happened at the certificate authority is not public. Go's announcement gives one sentence about security concerns, and the release came without the pre-announcement Go sent before its October 8 security releases. Go's security policy defines URGENT track issues as "a threat to the Go ecosystem's integrity" or flaws being actively exploited with severe damage, and says there are no recent examples. Go has not said which of those applied. On the issue, one user asked for the committed patch to explain "who and what they correspond to." The Go team had not replied as of October 20. eMudhra is an Indian certificate authority that sells certificates under the emSign brand. Its roots emSign Root CA - G1 and emSign ECC Root CA - G3 are in the Chrome, Apple , and Mozilla root stores. The company told Mozilla earlier this year that its newer TLS root is cross-signed by emSign Root CA - G1, which is how certificates under the newer root chain to a trusted root. In September, a six-week public discussion of eMudhra's request to add ten new roots to the root programs run by browser and operating-system makers, including emSign Root TLS CA - G3, closed with no objections. Certificates logged for eMudhra's own domains, including emsign.com and emudhra.com, chain through other eMudhra intermediates, according to certificate transparency records The Hacker News checked on October 20. The company's repository contained no notice about the intermediates as of that day, and The Hacker News found no public statement from eMudhra. Go 1.25 and older releases are out of support and get no fixes, so the only route is a supported release from the download page. No temporary workaround exists in any source, and the filter cannot be disabled. Sites and services whose certificates chain through the eight keys will need certificates from a different intermediate before rebuilt Go clients can connect to them.

1wtavno.text: French cloud and hosting provider OVHcloud is warning users that attackers compromised its open-source command-line interface (CLI) tool to distribute information-stealing malware. The attacker hijacked a developer’s GitHub account to gain access to the OVHcloud CLI repository and modify versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 of the tool. OVHcloud offers the CLI tool as an alternative for system administrators and developers to manage cloud and hosting services directly from a terminal, including for automating tasks. OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba disclosed that the company’s CLI repository on GitHub had been compromised, urging users who downloaded the latest version yesterday to update or remove the tool. Klaba said that the compromised release appeared at 14:47 on October 19 and was detected and blocked at 16:21 after a customer reported it. "The compromised versions are v0.11.0 v0.12.0 v0.13.0 v0.14.0 v0.15.0," the CEO said, adding that older version 0.10.0 and the latest release 0.16.0 were clean. Despite the poor quality of the malware, its purpose was to "retrieve secrets from the disk," Klaba explained. In a later update, Klaba shared that GitHub’s release immutability setting was disabled, allowing a sufficiently privileged account to modify existing releases without passing CI/CD checks. "The entire set of CI/CD pipelines with unit tests, functional tests, CVE detection, etc., were not impacted." OVHcloud has enabled GitHub’s release immutability feature and considers the incident resolved. However, Klaba urges users who downloaded a compromised CLI package to perform a system cleanup and revoke all secrets. "The quality of the binary is poor but it can go all the way. If you are affected, please change all the secrets on your disk." GlassWorm connection According to OpenSourceMalware, a community-driven threat intelligence platform, the attack was likely part of a new GlassWorm operation, known for campaigns since late 2025 that impacted the VSCode, OpenVSX, GitHub, and npm software development ecosystems. The researchers confirmed that the attacker did not tamper with the CI/CD pipelines and uploaded malware-infected packages built locally. OVHcloud CLI compromise overviewSource: OpenSourceMalware The researchers note that the GitHub account used in the attack had been compromised for more than half a year. "Its public repositories show a scripted history rewrite on 5 March 2026 and a hidden preinstall.js loader that decodes to a second stage using a Solana memo dead drop," OpenSourceMalware researchers found. Although the associated wallet is a known GlassWorm indicator, the researchers did not analyze the malicious payload delivered through a trojanized version of the OVHcloud CLI. According to OpenSourceMalware's report, affected platforms are macOS (Intel and ARM), Linux (x86_64 and ARM64), and Windows x86-64. Source builds and Docker images remained unaffected. Anyone who ran an affected binary should treat all secrets on the machine as compromised. ebxz0v.text: Ahold Delhaize, one of the world's largest food retail chains, confirmed that last week's cyberattack disrupted services at stores across Europe and the United States. Right before the cyberattack was disclosed, customers couldn't use websites, apps, and customer service platforms at Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall stores in the Netherlands, and Delhaize in Belgium, while employees at the Stop & Shop American regional supermarket chain reported having trouble accessing their schedules and pay stubs. When BleepingComputer asked right after the incident whether it also affected both corporate and store systems and whether any devices were encrypted during the attack, an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson redirected us to the company's statement. In a Monday update, Ahold Delhaize said the cybersecurity incident announced last week forced it to take some systems offline, including its brands' websites and apps, causing service issues, although stores remained open to serve customers. While most store websites and apps in Central and Southeastern Europe (CSE) are now online, the company says it's still working to restore some systems and services for European and US brands that remain down. "Albert Heijn's website and app are back online, with home deliveries expected to resume from Friday, October 23. The Etos and Gall & Gall websites are also available for customers. E-commerce services at our Ahold Delhaize USA brands are expected to come back in the coming days. In Belgium, e-commerce is now fully operational," Ahold Delhaize said. "As part of our response, we notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) within 24 hours of discovering the malicious activity and have continued to provide timely updates to the NCSC, law enforcement and other relevant regulatory authorities. Today, Ahold Delhaize has filed a formal police report with the Dutch police. The retail giant did not share further details that could interfere with response efforts or compromise security measures protecting its systems, but noted that an ongoing investigation has not yet found evidence that sensitive customer, associate, or partner data was stolen in the incident. "Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused - especially to our customers," said Frans Muller, President and CEO of Ahold Delhaize. This is the second major cyberattack to affect Ahold Delhaize's systems in recent years, after the personal, financial, and health information of over 2.2 million individuals was stolen in a November 2024 attack that impacted the company's U.S. systems and was claimed by the ransomware group INC Ransom. The multinational retailer employs more than 384,000 people and operates 9,551 stores serving 77 million customers each week across the United States, Europe, and Indonesia. 1086zvx.text: The Russia-linked state-sponsored threat actor tracked as APT28 (aka BlueDelta, Fancy Bear, and Forest Blizzard) has been attributed to attacks targeting two member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). The Symantec Threat Hunter Team, which is tracking the activity cluster under the moniker Swallowtail, involved the use of a backdoor called HOOKEDGE and a previously undocumented loader that is designed to decrypt and run an encrypted payload in memory by using a cryptographic key that's supplied at runtime. Targets of the activity included a law enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder, and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines – entities that hold information that could be of use to a foreign intelligence agency, the Broadcom-owned threat intelligence unit said. "During one attack against the naval shipbuilder, operators returned to a compromised host repeatedly over the course of a week in what appeared to be hands-on-keyboard activity," Symantec said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "They stole credential material using two separate techniques, opened a persistent SSH tunnel into the organization's internal network and deployed a previously undocumented reflective loader." APT28's use of HOOKEDGE was first publicly documented by Recorded Future Insikt Group in late August 2026 in connection with a cyber espionage campaign targeting government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain, and Türkiye between September 2025 and early April 2026. HOOKEDGE shares significant code and tradecraft overlap with HEADLACE, a modular Windows implant that APT28 has put to use in attacks targeting diplomats since April 2023. Delivered via spear-phishing lures, HOOKEDGE is a barebones Windows batch script that's capable of accepting attacker-issued commands and sending the results back. The backdoor is delivered via macro-enabled Microsoft Word documents and communicates entirely through a webhook[.]site URL, which acts as a channel to stage tasks and to receive execution output. Infected machines then fetch these tasks using a hidden, off-screen instance of the Microsoft Edge browser as opposed to relying on a traditional downloader. In the attack aimed at the naval shipbuilder in late July 2026, the threat actors are said to have delivered new variants of HOOKEDGE that abandon the use of webhook[.]site in favor of a dedicated IP address ("185.82.218[.]119:443") for both tasking and exfiltration. "The attackers used two distinct credential-theft techniques," Symantec said. "In one, they pushed an SSH private key onto the compromised host and immediately used it to open an SSH connection back to their own server, requesting a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that would give them a route from their infrastructure into the target's internal network." "In the other, they ran a short, self-contained PowerShell script that stands up a listener on the host's own loopback address and forces the machine to authenticate to it, capturing the resulting NTLM handshake." The attackers have also been observed dropping a new reflective loader ("ld.exe") using a curl command via SSH that's engineered to decode and run a next-stage component. The exact nature of the payload remains unknown. The most recent activity was registered on September 24, 2026, when a Visual Basic Script launcher associated with HOOKEDGE was observed within the shipbuilder's network. It's unclear if any data was stolen as a result of these intrusions. "The tradecraft observed after initial access, credential theft through two independent techniques, a persistent network tunnel, and a previously undocumented loader, goes beyond the delivery mechanism that has so far been publicly reported on this campaign," Symantec said. Attacks Targeting Ukraine in H1 2026 In a report published late last month, the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) revealed that Russian hackers are increasingly targeting the smartphones belonging to Ukrainian military personnel and government officials for espionage and financially motivated attacks. "The growing role of smartphones in communications among military personnel, government employees, and civilians is making them more attractive targets for intelligence gathering activity, further compromise, and financially motivated attacks," the agency said. This includes the use of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit, which is distributed via watering-hole attacks through compromised legitimate Ukrainian news outlets and government sites to siphon sensitive data from compromised devices. "The tool is associated with Russian threat actors, and its use against Ukrainian targets points to the adversary's growing interest in the iOS platform, which had previously been considered relatively secure," the agency noted. The findings are consistent with a report from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) in March 2026, which linked the Russian espionage actor UNC6353 to the use of Coruna and DarkSword kits in watering-hole campaigns targeting Ukrainian users since summer 2025. The threats also extend to the Android ecosystem, with threat clusters UAC-0244 and UAC-0263 using decoy apps to deliver two different malware families - UAC-0244 distributes CAMELSPY, which harvests device system information, geolocation, SIM card details, contacts, call logs, and images from the gallery. UAC-0263 distributes BTMOB RAT, which gives the threat actor control over the infected device and the ability to exfiltrate data. CERT-UA also said it observed APT28 exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-21509, a security feature bypass in Microsoft Office, and CVE-2026-8496, a zero-click vulnerability in the SOGo webmail client, to deliver the COVENANT malware as well as siphon victims' mailbox credentials and data, respectively. "At the same time, the actor has not abandoned older, tried-and-tested – but unfortunately still effective – approaches," CERT-UA said. "In particular, attacks exploiting XSS vulnerabilities in the Roundcube webmail client were observed. Excel documents containing macros were also used to further distribute COVENANT." These attacks are among the 3,137 cyber incidents recorded by CERT-UA in the first half of 2026, which is estimated to be 8% more than in the second half of 2025. The development comes as Team Cymru said it identified five additional LegionRelay command-and-control (C2) servers used in attacks targeting Ukrainian entities. The IP addresses are listed below - 91.149.221[.]118:8000 91.149.221[.]123:8000 166.88.239[.]54:8000 194.87.108[.]12:8000 194.87.108[.]217:8000 LegionRelay is the name assigned to a PowerShell-based RAT that supports file enumeration, file exfiltration, screenshot capture, browser data theft, Telegram and WhatsApp data exfiltration, and RDP access setup. It's attributed to a threat actor dubbed GREYVIBE, which is assessed to have engaged in persistent attacks targeting Ukraine and Ukraine-related entities since at least August 2025.

1obqsp.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Cloud Security / Incident Response ConnectWise on Monday said it has taken remediation measures, including strengthening administrative-access protections and resetting accounts and replacing application credentials, as it continues to respond to a security incident that led to unauthorized access to application identities associated with Cloud Backup. The company said it has completed the following actions since it began rolling out mitigations on October 17 at 5:00 a.m. UTC, three days after the incident was first identified - Disabling affected application connections and suspending Cloud Backup. Suspending SaaS Security and Cloud Management as a precaution because they are integrated with Cloud Backup. Enlisting the help of independent third-party specialists for incident response and remediation. Enhancing administrative-access protections. Publishing technical guidance to help partners investigate and remediate potential unauthorized activity in their own and managed customer environments. ConnectWise said it's validating the effectiveness of its containment measures and emphasized that it has not seen any successful threat activity in the environments it monitors. There is no evidence that any ConnectWise products and services, other than Cloud Backup and the precautionary suspensions of SaaS Security and Cloud Management, are impacted. "This observation does not establish whether individual partner or customer Microsoft 365 tenants have been affected," it said. "Reviewing each potentially affected tenant remains essential." "Before making changes, preserve relevant evidence, validate findings, and assess potential operational impacts. Completing these steps does not guarantee that a tenant is unaffected or that all unauthorized access has been eliminated. Do not reconnect affected applications until ConnectWise provides formal restoration instructions." Huntress has shared the following IP addresses observed in connection with the activity, adding that the password spray and failed login attempts linked to some of them are unlikely to be related to the application sign-in activity - 144.172.64[.]128 - Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector) 144.172.64[.]99 - Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14, 2026) 144.172.64[.]60 - A few failed user logins (October 18, 2026) 144.172.94[.]243 - Broad failed login spray, ongoing against many organizations "In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity," Huntress researchers said in an update. "We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them." The cybersecurity company said it also observed post-compromise actions on a second tenant, following the same modus operandi as before, in which the application granted itself Global Administrator and then added a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant for persistence. While the access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, there are no signs the attackers weaponized it for mailbox or file manipulation, or to make user or policy changes. "The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed," Huntress added. "Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do."

1wwf2h8.text: Fintech company Revolut is working to resolve a massive outage that disrupted most of its services worldwide earlier today. Since the incident began, thousands of users on the Downdetector outage tracking platform have reported issues with the Revolut app, mobile banking services, and transferring funds between accounts. In a statement today, the company said the outage has affected its services since Tuesday morning and added that customers' data and funds are safe. "We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," Revolut said. "We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused." On its official status page, the company says the outage affects 28 services, including sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading, and live support chat, which are now flagged as partially unavailable. Revolut status page (BleepingComputer) According to Reuters, the Revolut outage is reportedly linked to ongoing service ​disruptions affecting Google Cloud's London-based europe-west2 data center after a "power event." A Revolut spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer reached out earlier about the root cause of today's outage. Last month, Revolut also disclosed a data breach after it shared personally identifiable information (PII) from an undisclosed number of customers with a threat actor who was impersonating a government agency. Four years ago, Revolut disclosed another data breach after threat actors stole the personal, contact, and financial information of more than 50,000 customers in September 2022. Revolut provides banking, money management, and investment services to more than 80 million customers across 160+ countries and regions, including 800,000 business customers. 5botl.text: An attacker used a contributor's GitHub account to replace the download archives on five existing releases of OVHcloud's command-line tool on Monday, October 19. The account had been hijacked, and the new files were a build designed to steal secrets stored on the disk of any machine that runs it, the cloud provider says. They were live on GitHub for up to 94 minutes, from 12:47 to 14:21 UTC, and reached only people who installed or updated the OVHcloud CLI during that window, via a path that checks for no hash, on macOS, Linux x86_64 or arm64, or Windows x86_64. OVHcloud deleted the swapped archives and published a clean v0.16.0 that evening as an immutable release, whose files GitHub will not let anyone change. The source code, the release tag, and the company's build pipeline were not touched: the bad build was a plain go build of a later commit, uploaded straight onto releases published between April and September. Who Was Exposed On v0.15.0, the attacker replaced six files: the macOS x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Linux x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Windows x86_64 archive, and the checksums.txt file, so the published hashes matched the new binaries. The same six files are now gone from v0.11.0 to v0.14.0 as well. The Linux i386, Windows i386, Windows arm64, and WebAssembly builds were left alone on every release. OVHcloud lists v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 as compromised and v0.10.0 as clean. Those five releases were published between April 14 and September 16, so a copy installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and not updated since is the original. You got a swapped file if, in that window and on one of those platforms, you: Ran the official install script (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ovh/ovhcloud-cli/main/install.sh | sh). It downloads the latest release archive and installs it, and has never checked a hash. Downloaded an archive from the GitHub release page of any of the five releases. Ran a CI job or build step that fetches the archive from the release download URL without a pinned hash. Ran the CLI's own upgrade command from a v0.12.0, v0.13.0, or v0.14.0 install on a macOS or Linux machine where the tool was installed by the script or by hand. The command downloads the archive and replaces the binary with no hash check. On a Homebrew or go install setup it only prints the command to run instead. You did not get it if you: Installed with Homebrew, whose cask in force during the window pinned the original SHA-256 of each archive. Homebrew refuses a download whose hash does not match, so brew install or brew upgrade would have failed rather than installed the swapped file. Some early write-ups listed Homebrew among the exposed paths, but The Hacker News checked the tap's commit history: nothing changed between the v0.15.0 cask on September 16 and the v0.16.0 cask on Monday evening. Used go install or built from source. The v0.15.0 tag still points at its September commit, 760fd72. Pulled the Docker image. Its latest tag was last pushed on September 21, four weeks before the swap, and had not been rebuilt as of Tuesday. Installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and did not update during the window. How to Tell The customer who caught the swap pulled the build information out of the new v0.15.0 Linux arm64 binary with go version -m, which reads the file without running it, and posted it in a GitHub issue. Three things mark the bad build: The module line reads v0.15.1-0.20261013083505-5ead8ef9b43d+dirty, a pseudo-version, the stand-in string Go generates for a build from an untagged commit, here one from October 13. A genuine release carries its tag number: OVHcloud's clean v0.16.0 build reads v0.16.0+dirty. The recorded commit is 5ead8ef, not 760fd72, the commit the v0.15.0 tag points to. A -ldflags="-s -w" line is present. OVHcloud's release pipeline builds with a version flag that Go leaves out of the recorded flags, so a genuine release shows no -ldflags line at all. Advice circulating that any build marked +dirty, or carrying vcs lines, is the malicious one would flag OVHcloud's own release. The Hacker News ran the same command on the clean v0.16.0 Linux x86_64 binary: it reports v0.16.0+dirty, vcs.modified=true and the commit it was built from. The only published hash of a swapped file is the v0.15.0 Linux arm64 archive: SHA-256 (swapped archive): 3833daffcaaaab27e4e0e0833240ffcb1df8df648f4ec0bc4a75c176e28933cb SHA-256 (original archive): 5c2beb56e6d83a4b426565a1557791ef759316abcc4effb38dd627c90aeb80e0 A build without the version flag would report its version as undefined, but running a suspect binary to find out is not advisable. What to Do OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba wrote on X on Monday evening that anyone affected should change every secret stored on the disk. = The CLI keeps OVHcloud API credentials in ~/.ovh.conf and reads them from environment variables, according to its documentation, and the advice covers everything else on the disk, not only those files. If you ran a swapped build, or cannot tell, treat every secret readable from that machine as exposed and rotate it. OpenSourceMalware, which investigated the incident, adds: do it from a different machine. Remove the binary and install v0.16.0. The release is immutable and carries a release attestation, a signed record of its files. Updating replaces the program but does not revoke a key that was already copied, which is why the rotation comes first. Check a downloaded archive against the release with gh release verify-asset v0.16.0 FILE, as GitHub documents. OVHcloud has not said which files the binary reads, where it sends them, or how many copies were downloaded, and no copy of a swapped archive has been analyzed in public. The company has promised a detailed postmortem in the coming days. How It Happened Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can delete the files attached to a release and upload new ones with the same names, and the download URL does not change unless release immutability is enabled. The setting, generally available since October 2025, locks a release's files and tag but protects only releases created after it is enabled. OVHcloud had not enabled it. In a second post on Monday night, quoted by Next, Klaba wrote that the problem stemmed from the immutability option not being activated, so a user with the right permissions could modify existing releases directly on GitHub without any checks by the company's CI/CD pipeline. The option has now been enabled, and the pipelines themselves were not affected. The five old releases now offer only the four archives the attacker did not touch. The uploads came through the account of a contributor whose merged work is in OVHcloud's documentation repository and who is not a public member of the organization, according to OpenSourceMalware, which built a timeline from GitHub's server-side records. The release workflow never ran: the run list shows no workflow between October 16 and the v0.16.0 tag push at 16:00 UTC on Monday. First checks found no other repository affected, Klaba wrote in his first post, and OVHcloud has not said how the account's credentials were taken. A customer's CI job caught the swap because it pins the SHA-256 of the Linux arm64 archive and began failing. With no private reporting channel on the repository, the customer filed a public issue, at 13:50 UTC by OpenSourceMalware's timeline, and OVHcloud deleted the swapped files about half an hour later, at 14:21 UTC (16:21 in Paris). v0.16.0 followed at 17:16 UTC, published under the company's ovh-cds account with a signed tag. The GlassWorm Question OpenSourceMalware ties the account to GlassWorm, the malware campaign that hides code in invisible Unicode characters and fetches its next stage from the memo field of a Solana wallet's transactions. Four of the account's personal repositories were force-pushed on March 5 and 6 with an amended commit that added a loader of that kind, the researchers found. The wallet that loader reads is the one named in GlassWorm's ForceMemo campaign, which force-pushed malware into hundreds of Python repositories in March with stolen GitHub tokens. The Hacker News confirmed that the loader file is still in one of those repositories, with the hash the researchers published. Whether the same actor did both is "our inference," the researchers wrote. The shared account is the link, and nothing from the October binary has been tied to GlassWorm, because no copy of it was preserved.

1kvxe5v.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security Siemens has addressed a DLL sideloading vulnerability impacting Siemens Software Center that it said has been exploited in ClickFix attacks. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v4 score: 8.4), could allow an attacker to place a specially-crafted DLL in a directory the application searches, resulting in execution of malicious code with the same privileges as the affected service. "The affected application loads dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from an uncontrolled search path," Siemens said in an advisory. "This could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application." The issue has been patched in version 4.0.9.8. Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon has been credited with discovering and reporting the shortcoming. In a separate alert, Siemens said attackers have abused a genuine copy of Siemens Software Center with a valid signature and placed their own crafted DLL ("archive.dll") next to it to trigger the execution of malicious code. "They chose this program as a carrier because it is signed and trusted, and because version 3.5.8.7, the latest version at the time, loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them," Siemens added. Specifically, threat actors have been found leveraging "msiexec.exe" to launch "AllMyBasic.msi," which then executes "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe." The activity has been attributed to a ClickFix delivery platform called Romulus, which was detailed by Forescout last week as being used to deliver Legion Loader and other malware using DLL sideloading. According to Huntress, some of these campaigns have leveraged malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving a ClickFix lure, which when copied and executed by the victim, runs PowerShell code to drop an MSI installer that abuses DLL sideloading to ultimately deploy a remote access trojan. Siemens has shared the following indicators of compromise - 96.62.218[.]59 (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) wizardexpensive[.]com (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) 2.27.248[.]127 (Distribution channel of AllMyBasic.msi) Besides updating Siemens Software Center to version 4.0.9.8 or later and starting the application to apply the update, organizations are advised to block the IP addresses and domains associated with the malicious activity and look for "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe" running from "AppData\Local\Programs" and started by "msiexec.exe."

11e0hy4.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 20, 2026Cyber Espionage / Data Security A U.S. court on Monday granted the U.S. government's request to detain a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office to allegedly steal sensitive secrets. In a new court filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026. Alfozan is said to have communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as October 5, 2026, four days before he was arrested. "Among other things, the individual told the defendant that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing reads. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed." The Saudi Royal Family member is said to have repeatedly attempted to recruit Alfozan and even asked when he planned to leave OpenAI, to which the defendant said he wouldn't do so until his stock vested. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer around July 2025 with an annual base salary of $385,000. Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) revealed that he had been arrested for allegedly inserting a stealthy audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in the executive conference room to capture sensitive conversations. The defendant is also said to have modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television and encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD card. In addition, he used his wife's personal ChatGPT account to research how to "build a continuous audio recorder" to "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card." "In the days and weeks before placing the device, the defendant (i) used an OpenAI productivity agent to ascertain which 'meeting rooms' OpenAI 'leadership and exec[utives]' used, and where they met with 'external partners'; and (ii) spent considerable time near the conference room where he later installed the device," the filing said. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison. Prosecutors also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk, stating he has "ample resources... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance," according to the filing. Shortly after details of his arrest became public knowledge, it emerged that the defendant had planned to depart to Riyadh with his wife and son on a one-way ticket on October 12, 2026. Although he was arrested three days prior, his wife and son are said to have already left the U.S. without him. The day before her departure, Alfozan's wife allegedly told the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents that her U.S. visa was expiring and that she, along with her son, were permanently shifting back to Saudi Arabia. "The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in – and making plans to travel to – Saudi Arabia," the filing said. Stating the U.S. government's investigation is ongoing, prosecutors said a search of the defendant's residence and a "preliminary review" of his electronic devices, including his cellphone, uncovered several pieces of evidence - Several electronic components similar to those in the customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room and had in his missing bag were identified in his residence. Photographs from his iPhone dated between September 22 and 28, 2026, that depict one additional concealed recording device, as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on TVs and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including a second conference room where sensitive meetings took place. A deleted note on his cellphone from September 2026 included links to various recording devices, including those made by Seeed Studio, the same manufacturer whose devices were found in OpenAI's offices and his residence. Browsing history showed that the defendant accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on October 4, 2026, and he used an OpenAI productivity agent to inquire about various Saudi-related business and government-related engagements from the Saudi Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MCIT) between July 6, 2026, and September 21, 2026. "The defendant leveraged his skills as a highly-educated engineer to create sophisticated recording devices that – the evidence strongly suggests – he intended to bring with him to Saudi Arabia," the filing said. "Whether the defendant wanted to record OpenAI meetings to enrich himself by enhancing his own business prospects, or to provide aid a foreign government, or both, his conduct is criminal and it presents a danger to innovation in the Silicon Valley and a concern for the national security of the United States."

lre2pv.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybercrime Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a ClickFix delivery platform called ROMULUS that's being used to distribute malware such as Legion Loader. According to Forescout Research - Vedere Labs, ROMULUS is akin to a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures on bogus landing pages to trick unsuspecting users into running malicious commands and infecting their own machines. "ROMULUS may be a privately operated panel, a commercial cybercriminal delivery service, an affiliate framework, or software that has been copied between operators," security researcher Sai Molige said in an analysis. The cybersecurity company said it identified six IP addresses running ROMULUS - 96.62.224[.]81 86.109.75[.]7 151.240.151[.]223 23.94.145[.]224 93.152.224[.]118 2.27.248[.]127 Notably, the IP address "96.62.224[.]81" was identified as hosting a ClickFix script and an MSI installer file in connection with another campaign that has been found to leverage malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving the ClickFix lure. Forescout's own analysis has since uncovered the same malware being delivered via another server, 86.109.75[.]7, that also hosted a panel codenamed ROMULUS. In addition, a separate chain triggered via ClickFix has been used to run a PowerShell script, which then delivers Legion Loader, a malware loader also called Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper. As of writing, it's not known who is behind the ROMULUS platform. However, it shares no overlaps with RomulusLoader, a malware family associated with Silver Fox (aka TA4922), a China-aligned threat actor known for repeatedly using tax-related pretexts to distribute remote access trojans like ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0), DcRAT, and potentially Venom RAT via DLL sideloading techniques. The ROMULUS platform exposes two endpoints that are designed to download a PowerShell staging script, which decides the payload to be fetched next: a trojanized MSI installer carrying a malware loader or an encrypted archive containing Legion Loader that's inflated to nearly 1 GB with repetitive padding to bypass upload limits, sandbox budgets, or static-analysis thresholds. The loader, for its part, communicates with a remote server to fetch and run additional payloads. The findings indicate how ClickFix is evolving beyond a social engineering technique into a highly effective entry point for malware. To mitigate the threat, it's essential to hunt for suspicious PowerShell commands and DLL sideloading events.

18i6r84.text: Nikkei Inc. disclosed a new data breach, the third in about a month, that exposed 1.83 million personal information records. The Japanese giant says subsets of the data contained personally identifiable information and other sensitive details, but most records contained no identifying info. The company said that 150,000 records contained at least one of the following data types: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in 120,000 records. The remaining 1.68 million records contain no identifiers, the company said, and no credit card information was exposed. Nikkei Inc. is a major Japanese business news and financial information group, owner of Financial Times, the country’s largest business-focused media company. The company employs over 10,100 people and has an annual revenue of $2.5 billion (¥393.8 billion). According to a notice Nikkei published late last week, hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within its network during the early morning hours of October 7. The unauthorized access exposed personal information the company stored in the cloud. Nikkei revoked the abused credentials and notified the Personal Information Protection Commission on October 11. The company is currently examining the scope of the breach and noted that as of October 16, it had no evidence that the accessed information was misused or leaked online. The company has also found no signs of system compromise or data tampering resulting from this incident, and has experienced no service outages. The firm said those affected will receive individual notifications. “We are working urgently to establish the extent of the damage and determine the cause, and will implement the necessary measures to strengthen security,” Nikkei stated. This is the third cybersecurity incident that Nikkei disclosed recently. Earlier this month, the company disclosed a breach that occurred in late July, when hackers compromised an employee's Google Workspace account and accessed personal information belonging to employees and business partners. In September, Nikkei announced that threat actors hijacked another employee’s Microsoft 365 account and used it to send spear-phishing emails to the firm’s staff. BleepingComputer has contacted Nikkei for more information about the latest breach, and we will update this post once we receive a response. 1hdbrk3.text: Some downloads of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin from the vendor’s official website carried malware that planted hidden backdoors in a supply-chain attack last week. According to the vendor, a limited number of users who downloaded version 3.0.123 of the plugin between October 15 at 20:02 UTC and October 16 at 07:12 UTC received compromised versions that could compromise their websites upon activation. “The affected plugin files contained malware that could compromise your website if the plugin was activated,” Rank Math warned. “We immediately removed the affected files and released a clean version, Rank Math PRO v3.0.124.” Users who installed and activated the trojanized version during this 11-hour window should treat their websites as compromised and follow the clean-up procedures in the advisory from the vendor. Rank Math PRO is a WordPress search engine optimization (SEO) plugin that helps websites improve visibility in search results. It is the paid version of the free variant that is active on more than 4 million websites. Sensitive material exposed An advisory from the vendor highlights that only the PRO version was compromised and the free version of Rank Math SEO from WordPress.org remained unaffected. Rank Math says that the malware establishes persistent access, communicates with ‘rank1cdn[.]com,’ and recreates hidden backdoors when someone visits the infected website. The vendor warns that users installing the compromised version of Rank Math PRO expose database credentials, API keys, and other secrets accessible to the web server. While researching the attack, BleepingComputer discovered a PHP malware sample on VirusTotal named 'cache-preloader-fff033 (1).php' that appears to be connected to the Rank Math compromise. Although this file was not mentioned in the Rank Math or Wordfence advisories, BleepingComputer found it contained the same indicators of compromise (IoCs) included in Rank Math's alert: xmmqhn' XOR obfuscation key the '_np5pvf754c' WordPress database entry the '#ms6v46' cron job marker code for creating administrator accounts using the 'wpsupport_' username prefix and '@wp-mail.net' email addresses The malware appears to act as a first-stage deployment script that creates the 'wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php' backdoor mentioned in Rank Math's advisory. The PHP script also includes the ability to execute commands, modify WordPress databases, and steal AWS, Cloudflare, Google Cloud, Azure credentials, SSH keys, and other sensitive information. While these IoCs indicate it is connected to the same threat actor as the Rank Math attack, BleepingComputer could not confirm whether it was distributed through the compromised plugin. Cleanup recommendations Website administrators who suspect a compromise should restore website files and the database from a clean backup, run security scans, and rotate all passwords, keys, and salts. For websites without a safe backup to restore from, Rank Math recommends manual cleanup, noting that deactivating or updating the plugin after a compromise will not remove the threat. Cleanup requires deleting the entire plugin folder and malicious database entries before investigating additional backdoors, unauthorized administrator accounts, altered files, scheduled tasks, and possible changes outside WordPress. It is also recommended to block all outbound connections to the attacker's rank1cdn[.]com domain. Users who installed but never activated the plugin should now delete it, download the clean 3.0.124 version, and then scan their sites. BleepingComputer contacted Rank Math for details on the number of potentially affected sites and the initial attack vector but had received no response by the time of publication. 1dr4wxj.text: Hackers reportedly compromised AOMEI's servers to distribute malware through a built-in promotional feature in its backup software, briefly tampering with configuration files before restoring them to their original state to hide the attacks. The supply chain attacks took place between April and July 2026 and targeted the update and notification systems used by AOMEI Backupper, a Windows application for backing up data, cloning disks, and restoring systems. Researchers at ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), working with Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign and investigated the attacks. In reports published by Google and ManageEngine, the activity is attributed to a threat actor tracked as UNC7017, who used the compromised infrastructure to distribute a previously unknown malware downloader called CROSSROAD and a backdoor named SHINYROAD. The researchers identified affected organizations in multiple countries, including the United States, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain, and Switzerland, across sectors such as IT services, telecommunications, and higher education. However, Google warned that the attacks were opportunistic and could have affected additional organizations that checked for software updates during the brief periods when malicious files were being distributed. Software The attacks were first detected on May 28, when ManageEngine said its endpoint security software spotted AOMEI Backupper suddenly installing the legitimate remote administration tool Radmin on computers at two unrelated companies in different countries. The Radmin installation was suspicious because AOMEI's built-in promotion processes launched it, which normally handle downloading and displaying promotional content and notifications. However, when researchers attempted to reproduce the behavior on their own test systems, they found nothing malicious. Instead, the software contacted AOMEI's servers and downloaded the legitimate configuration file. Further testing showed that instead of permanently replacing files on AOMEI's servers, the attackers briefly modified two configuration files used by the promotion and notification systems: https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini The first file, down_html.ini, tells AOMEI Backupper where to download update packages. The second, Notifycfg.ini, controls notifications and can trigger content to run on the computer. By modifying these files, the attackers redirected the software to download a malicious ZIP archive and then used the notification mechanism to execute the malware without requiring user interaction. Researchers at Google later confirmed this execution flow in their own tests. AOMEI supply chain attack execution flowSource: Google After failing to reproduce the original attack, ManageEngine began continuously monitoring AOMEI's servers. On July 16, that monitoring finally captured the malicious modifications as they happened, confirming that AOMEI's systems were serving the malicious content. The researchers also found that the attackers had modified the expected checksum in the update configuration, allowing the malicious archive to pass the software's file verification checks. Google and ManageEngine say they identified three windows where the malicious configuration file was being sent by Aomei's servers: May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC) July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC) July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC) The attackers restored the configuration files back to its original form within minutes, making the compromise difficult to detect. During these windows, the malicious configuration file was used to install the CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD malware. When launched, the CROSSROAD downloader checked the performed reconnasaince on the infected computer, downloaded additional components, and established persistence through a scheduled task. SHINYROAD is a backdoor that used legitimate Radmin components to load malicious code and establish an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled command-and-control server. This allowed the attackers to potentially execute additional commands and payloads on compromised computers. During the July 20 attack, Google also observed a second technique that attempted to steal Windows authentication hashes by forcing the software's notification system to access an attacker-controlled WebDAV resource through an invisible popup. This technique could expose NTLM hashes that can be collected by the attacker-controlled server and later cracked using various tools. The researchers also identified several IP addresses and hostnames used during the attacks, including 8.210.84[.]56, serv.oss-cn-hongkong[.]aliyuncs.com, hostnames under storage-data[.]com, and storage.googleapis.com, a legitimate Google Cloud Storage endpoint. AOMEI says CTO is investigating ManageEngine told BleepingComputer that it first notified AOMEI about the suspicious activity on June 7, more than a month before researchers directly captured the malicious configuration files being served from its servers. At the time, AOMEI initially suggested that the content may have been intercepted and modified while in transit, an explanation the researchers disagreed with. "The evidence did not support AOMEI’s explanation of interception in transit," reads ManageEngine's report. "Both endpoints had retrieved the content over HTTPS from AOMEI-owned hostnames, across different countries and unrelated network paths, and the executable had arrived through the application’s own extraction sequence rather than being written directly to disk by an external process. The content had been altered before it reached either endpoint, within the vendor-hosted delivery path." When ManageEngine captured another attack on July 16, it immediately provided AOMEI with the original and modified file hashes, file differences, and altered files. "AOMEI engaged, conducted its own review, and told us its initial examination had not found evidence of a breach," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer. The researchers said AOMEI indicated that it planned to move the affected configuration files to new infrastructure with more detailed logging. ManageEngine told BleepingComputer it advised AOMEI to preserve existing evidence before making those changes and to bring in incident-response specialists, connecting the company with Mandiant to assist with the investigation. AOMEI later informed the researchers that its technical team had upgraded its servers, patched potential vulnerabilities, and verified that the files hosted on its infrastructure were correct. Google also confirmed in its report that Mandiant notified AOMEI about the configuration file tampering on July 17 and that the company responded on July 29th, stating it took corrective action. When contacted by BleepingComputer about the findings, AOMEI said it was treating the matter as a high priority and that its chief technology officer was leading an internal investigation. "We have also internally detected this report and have classified it as a high-priority matter. Our CTO is currently leading a dedicated investigation to ensure accurate issue identification," AOMEI told BleepingComputer. The company said its CTO would provide a more detailed response about the incident and the investigation's progress, and BleepingComputer will update this article if we receive new information. AOMEI did not immediately confirm how attackers gained access to its update infrastructure or whether the reported compromise had been fully resolved. While AOMEI says it has secured its servers, ManageEngine warns that these changes would not remove malware previously installed on customers' computers. "A server-side fix stops new infections; it does not remove the backdoor from machines that received it during an earlier window," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer. Organizations using AOMEI Backupper are advised to review the indicators of compromise published by Google and ManageEngine, including suspicious scheduled tasks, unexpected executable files in AOMEI installation directories, and connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
