14m48xt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public. According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are below - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice. CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token. CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter. CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that allows the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it. Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances. The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks led to the deployment of a miner payload from a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116"). The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses - 91.92.40[.]202 176.65.139[.]228 45.194.92[.]222 176.65.139[.]228 Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog - Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic. Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet. Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws. The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws. It's unclear if the aforementioned vulnerabilities were part of this alert. The Hacker News has contacted Plex for comment and we will update the story if we hear back. In light of active exploitation, users are advised to keep their Plex installations up-to-date for optimal protection.

1v2pf25.text: Copies of Rank Math PRO, the paid version of the Rank Math SEO plugin for WordPress, that were downloaded from rankmath.com or delivered as updates between 20:02 UTC on October 15 and 07:12 UTC on October 16 contained malware, Rank Math said in a security notice published on October 16. Any site that installed and activated one of those copies should be treated as compromised, and the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site. Rank Math has removed the affected files and released a clean version, 3.0.124. Installing it replaces the plugin but does not remove files, administrator accounts, or scheduled tasks the malware may already have placed elsewhere on the server, Wordfence said in an advisory on October 17. Who Is Affected The version number does not show whether a copy is affected. Rank Math's changelog dates 3.0.123 to October 7, more than a week before the window opened, and the notice limits the incident to copies downloaded or installed through an update during the window. A copy of 3.0.123 obtained before 20:02 UTC on October 15 is outside it. The notice sorts sites into three cases: You installed and activated 3.0.123 during the window: treat the site as compromised, even if it has since been updated to 3.0.124, and follow the recovery steps below. You installed it but never activated it: delete the plugin files, install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account, and run a security scan. You downloaded it but never installed or activated it: nothing in this incident alone indicates the site was compromised. Rank Math has emailed some users about the incident and told anyone unsure whether the files were installed or activated to contact its support team. The notice applies only to the PRO plugin, which customers download and update from rankmath.com rather than WordPress.org. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org, which lists more than 4 million active installations and was last updated on October 6, is not named in it. What the Malware Does What is known about the malware comes from Rank Math's notice. Neither it nor Wordfence's advisory includes an analysis of the code, and neither names who is behind it. Deleting suspicious files before stopping what recreates the backdoor may not resolve the problem, which is why the cleanup order below matters. The attacker may also have left PHP backdoor files in other plugins' folders, in theme folders, and in the must-use plugins directory, created administrator accounts, added a fake WordPress core file, changed .htaccess so that .cache files run as PHP, and added scheduled tasks and SSH keys. Any password, database credential, API key, or other secret the site could reach may have been exposed, and owners should assume it was. Wordfence assigned the incident CVE-2026-111862 and rates it 9.8 out of 10, with the researcher listed as unknown. Patchstack classifies it as a backdoor and says that, because the attack was on Rank Math's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation." How to Recover Rank Math's preferred recovery is a restore. Where a backup of the site and its database from before 20:02 UTC on October 15 exists, restore it, run a security scan, change every password and credential, and only then install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account. Where no clean backup exists, the manual cleanup runs in a fixed order, and three actions come before anything else is touched: Delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder using the hosting file manager or FTP. "Deactivating the plugin alone is not sufficient," the notice says. In the wp_options table, delete any entry whose option_name is _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb or _np5pvf754c. Block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com if the hosting provider or firewall allows it. Only then does the search for other changes begin, in these places: Files: PHP files in wp-content/mu-plugins/, in other plugins' folders, in the inc/, includes/ and lib/ folders of non-default themes, in Rank Math's own includes/ folder, and in uploads/. Code: PHP that uses base64_decode with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open, or PHP-FPM socket code. File: wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, which is not a WordPress core file. Accounts: administrator usernames beginning wpsupport_, or accounts with email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net. Server: .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, .cache files containing PHP code, entries tagged #ms6v46 in the web server user's crontab, WordPress scheduled events, SSH authorized_keys files, other users' crontabs, running processes, and any location outside the site where the web server can write. Wordfence adds a caution: "Their absence does not, by itself, prove that a website is clean." Credentials are changed in every case, even after a restore from backup. The list covers WordPress passwords, the database username and password in wp-config.php, the security keys and salts in the same file, payment gateway, SMTP and other API keys, hosting control panel, FTP, SFTP and SSH access, secrets held in environment variables, and two-factor authentication for administrators. The cleanup ends with a security scan, wp core verify-checksums for WordPress core, and wp plugin verify-checksums --all, with the caution that checksums may not exist for premium plugins. WordPress.org publishes none for this one. The Hacker News checked its plugin-checksums service on October 19 and found no file for the PRO plugin under either of its names, while the service does publish one for the free plugin. The fallback notice provides a clean copy from the official source. The clean 3.0.124 goes on last, downloaded by logging in at rankmath.com directly. Some customers may be unable to log in and may need to reset their account password, the notice says, without saying why, and Rank Math will never send login or download links by email. What Rank Math Has Not Said Rank Math, part of the Swedish hosting group group.one, has not said how the malicious files entered its download and update system, how many customers received one, whether automatic updates delivered them, or what the clean and tainted packages' hashes are. Its only statement about the future is that the team is taking steps to reduce the risk of similar incidents. Registry records show the domain Rank Math tells owners to block, rank1cdn[.]com, was registered at 19:31 UTC on October 14, about a day before the window opened. A Pattern This Year This is at least the third time this year that a premium WordPress plugin's vendor-run update channel has delivered backdoored builds. In April, Nextend's update system served a backdoored Smart Slider 3 Pro for about six hours. In June, ShapedPlugin's Pro plugins were found to have been backdoored in its update channel, and one package that had shipped clean was later "tampered with under the same version number," the trap Rank Math's customers now face. Attackers also altered scripts served from Awesome Motive's CDN in June and poisoned BdThemes' API feed in August. Nothing published links the attackers behind any of those incidents to this one.

istocc.text: The worst problems don't always come with a warning. Sometimes they arrive through a service everyone trusts, a device someone bought, or a system nobody thought to check. By the time something looks wrong, the damage may already be done. This week had plenty of that. Trusted connections became a problem. Hardware wasn't as safe as it looked. Old bugs found new victims, and some systems were left so exposed that breaking in barely required any effort. Even AI agents crossed lines they weren't supposed to. Some attacks were clever. Others were painfully simple. The full recap shows just how much can go wrong, and how little it sometimes takes. ⚡ Threat of the Week ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup Following Unauthorized Access — ConnectWise disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. 🔔 Top News BeyondTrust Remote Support Flaw Exploited as 0-Day — The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. According to Google-owned Mandiant, the attack involved the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and a tunneling program called BARECLAW to route traffic through the device. Only a small number of organizations are assessed to be impacted. Microsoft Disrupts 3 Phishing Kits Linked to Over 1 Billion Scam Messages — Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace that sold three phishing kits, namely CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System, that were responsible for sending over 1 billion malicious messages to more than 75,000 organizations worldwide. Redmond said it took down Yam Store (aka Storm-3119), a coordinated underground network that offered commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkits that allowed other threat actors to readily purchase and deploy phishing pages and steal data and credentials. The kits were also capable of advanced evasion, such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Yam Store functioned as an initial access broker, peddling not just phishing kits but also infrastructure built on compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft and Google cloud environments. Ledger Finds Unauthorized Hardware Implants — Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis and other third-party resellers in Southeast Asia and Germany after a backdoor embedded into a handful of wallets led to the theft of an estimated $100 million in cryptocurrency. The implants are said to be an advanced version of a backdoor that hardware hacker Joe Grand found earlier this year and notified Ledger in March 2026. It's not clear how this occurred, but signs point to a compromise of Ledger's supply chain. One of the victims of the incident is a fraudster who engaged in a task scam and lost more than $4.8 million. "In this task scam, people were paid to fake sales and reviews of real items," Chainalysis said. "Then a 'negative balance' appeared, and they were told to add their own money in order to get paid. On Sep 22, the person behind the scam moved the proceeds into three separate Ledger addresses. On Oct 9, thieves emptied all three. One transfer each, into the same wallet." According to cybersecurity journalist Kim Zetter, Trezor wallet devices sold by third-party non-authorized sellers have also been found to contain implants that generated pre-determined seed phrases so as to allow the attackers to guess them easily and gain access to the accounts. Pwn2Own Ireland Demos 98 0-Days — The Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 hacking contest saw white-hat hackers exploiting 98 zero-day flaws, earning them a collective $1,262,000 in rewards. Ikotas Labs came first with 42.5 Master of Pwn points and $361,000 in cash after discovering 12 unique bugs. Xint and Team ZyGoat secured second and third spots. Ikotas Labs, Xint, and Mobile Hacking Lab broke into Google's Pixel 10, earning them $150,000, $300,000, and $112,500, respectively. Vendors are expected to patch the zero-days disclosed during the competition within 90 days before the details are publicly disclosed. OpenAI Disclosed New Misalignment Cases — OpenAI said internal models hacked more websites, bypassed browsing restrictions, and used cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn't otherwise access, in the latest set of disclosures where its agents carried out unethical and likely illegal acts. In all, the company reported seven new incidents. The development came as the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it received "multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers" whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, accessed personal data from Indian organizations. The agents found their way in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations. OpenAI Engineer Charged — The U.S. Department of Justice charged an OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, with attempting to intercept oral communications after allegedly planting a recording device in an executive conference room. Prosecutors claimed company security staff found a second device in his bag. CCTV footage placed the defendant near the conference room on several dates. Alfozan allegedly had no authority to access or participate in meetings held in the room, which is often reserved for the highest-level discussions. In a subsequent filing, federal prosecutors revealed that Alfozan had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest on October 9, 2026. Attacks on French Refrigeration Systems — Cyber attacks on Danfoss- and Copeland-managed refrigeration systems pushed temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F) for roughly six hours, impacting over 700 French supermarkets and forcing them to discard food. French cybersecurity authorities advised supermarkets to disconnect them from the internet. The attacks targeted Intermarché and Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc. The affected systems are said to be internet-facing and running outdated firmware. "The username is admin and the password changes every day automatically to.. the current date," security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. "Every single one is like this. You can just log in and change the temperature. Anybody can do it, easily scriptable." To make matters worse, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create an allowlist of trusted IP addresses permitted to log in. "Two things would have changed the outcome," Pen Test Partners said. "Cyber hygiene would have prevented the access: take the controller off the public internet, put remote access behind a VPN and an IP allowlist, bring third-party kit onto the network in a controlled, owned and documented way rather than leaving it on a contractor's own connection, change known and default credentials, and patch to a current release." Multiple vulnerabilities have been disclosed in the affected models, with Claroty warning that the issues could be exploited to "defrost the food." Collabora RCE Flaw Exploited to Backdoor Nextcloud Servers — Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2), in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud to backdoor servers. It has been patched in version 26.4.303. The attacks involve issuing a malicious request to the app's "proxy.php" endpoint to trigger command injection and plant a PHP web shell with the end goal of conducting reconnaissance and searching for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. Secure), and multiple vulnerabilities in Google BoringSSL. 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars How to Find Hidden AI Agents on Employee Devices and Bring Them Under Control → AI agents are quietly becoming a new insider threat, gaining access to company data, credentials, and internal systems without adequate security oversight. Join this webinar to learn how to uncover hidden AI agents on employee devices, detect malicious agent skills, identify risky permissions, and put practical controls in place before they lead to a security incident. How to Find Security Gaps and Build Faster Defenses Against AI-Powered Cyberattacks → AI-powered cyberattacks are evolving faster than traditional defenses can keep up. Join this webinar to learn how to assess your organization's AI threat readiness, uncover critical security gaps, strengthen detection and response capabilities, and build a practical defense strategy against emerging AI-driven threats. 📰 Around the Cyber World Meta said it addressed an issue after reports emerged that some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people's conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the "Hey, Meta" prompt phrase. "This issue has been resolved," Meta told Android Authority. "People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time." Meta did not say what caused the smart glasses to record people without user consent, or how many of them were affected. Fortra said it's tracking a 12-fold increase in emails using requests for quotation, project invitations, and procurement inquiries as phishing lures from October 2025 to September 2026. "These messages impersonate prospective buyers seeking pricing, availability, or project participation," Fortra said. "Their purpose is not to obtain a legitimate quote, but to persuade a recipient to access an attacker-controlled file-sharing, document-viewing, or procurement portal." A fake download site for the WatchGuard Mobile VPN with SSL ("watchguard-vpn[.]net") has been observed using a browser pop-up prompt to steal the victim's VPN server address, username, and password. As of October 13, the domain was offline. "In a unique twist, after collecting credentials twice (the first attempt gets rejected as 'incorrect' in a likely attempt to collect multiple credentials), the site then downloads the genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer directly from WatchGuard's own content delivery network (CDN), meaning there is no malicious file for endpoint security tools to flag," Huntress said. "Meanwhile, unbeknownst to the victim, the threat actor now has access to their credentials, giving them access to victims' networks." A set of 42 malicious RubyGems packages has used typosquatting, brandjacking, and plausible utility names to target cryptocurrency and Web3 developers. The packages are designed to spawn a reverse shell and download a crypto theft kit capable of rerouting cryptocurrency transactions by replacing the destination address with an attacker-controlled wallet and harvesting wallet material, such as seed phrases and private keys. The names of some of the packages are: lightinng-invoice, cryoto-toolbox, etheremu.rb, bitcoin-rpc-lite, web3-sign-helper, and crypto-mnemonic-tools. The activity has been codenamed Ghost Dev by Open Source Malware. GreyNoise said it has observed a spike in scanning and exploitation attempts targeting Digital Video Recorders (DVRs) in Ukraine between September 21 and October 1, 2026. The majority of the activity attempts to exploit CVE-2021-36260, which allows unauthenticated command injection against unpatched Hikvision products. A series of email campaigns have been targeting the accommodation industry with fake guest complaints or reviews that deliver blockchain technology-abusing malware. "These emails appear to likely be a continuation of a prior series of predominantly Booking.com-spoofing emails that were seen delivering various remote access trojans (RAT) via ClickFix fake CAPTCHA websites," Cofense said. The activity leveraged the Ethereum and TON blockchains, a technique called EtherHiding, to deliver EtherRAT and TONResolver malware. As AI agents increasingly are being used to automate coding workflows, it increases the risk associated with credential exposure, Trellix warned. "Agents constantly take credentials out of the safe places your operating system keeps them, and put them somewhere far more exposed," Trellix said. "This happens as a normal side effect of everyday work. And even good security telemetry has a hard time distinguishing this from a developer doing their job -- or from an attacker who is already inside." MITRE released version 20 of its ATT&CK framework, adding entries that cover AI abuse, MFA bypass, and recent attacks on water utilities. This includes nine new Techniques and Sub-Techniques under the Enterprise domain for prompt injection, AI-enabled exfiltration, AI result poisoning, attacks on AI-assisted defenses, CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) evasion, and application-specific password theft. For Mobile, MITRE also un-deprecated a technique for delivering malicious apps outside official app stores, last included in v11. Fake AI tool campaigns that impersonate Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, and other AI brands are being used to plant infostealers on compromised systems using ClickFix lures. Some of the prominent targets include the U.S. and India. "The attacks share one trait: the employee performs the decisive step," ANY.RUN said. "They paste an 'install command,' run a convincing installer, or sign in to a fake window. That can put source code, cloud and AI API keys, active business sessions, ad accounts, and billing access at risk, turning a single user action into potential data exposure, account compromise, financial loss, or disruption to development and marketing operations." An official OpenAI skill, render-deploy, suffered from a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability which instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain ("render-internal[.]com"). "It builds apps that trust a domain nobody owns, so any attacker could register it and start receiving tokens from real production apps," AIR Security said. "Vulnerable servers in the wild sent tokens to the domain, users are advised to update to the patched version of the skill." The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned that scammers could exploit the 2026 U.S. midterm election to perpetrate financial fraud schemes. "As previously reported, scammers use the names, images, logos, and slogans of candidates to fraudulently solicit campaign contributions, sell merchandise that is never delivered, or steal personally identifiable information (PII) that can be used for other fraud," the FBI said. 1vhzwlm.text: The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file. The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running. According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow. The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. It's unclear if the latter code-hosting-themed domain is operated by the same threat actor. "It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered." Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer the same day it was registered. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com," warned of a new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account. The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack. The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data. The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443. "The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session." "The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session." By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/." "The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said. To make matters worse, the campaign has also been observed incorporating a second-stage component that persists on developer machines even after the malicious workflow has been removed. Specifically, the approach takes a leaf out of North Korea's playbook by committing three different files - A Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json file with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger that causes it to run automatically when the folder is opened in the application. A "public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2" file that contains a stealer payload designed to harvest AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git logins, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The font file name is the same as one used in North Korea's PolinRider campaign from January 2026. A second GitHub Actions workflow that's activated if the infostealer never runs. This causes VS Code to auto-run the credential stealer, which, besides collecting data, installs a cron job that runs attacker-supplied code every five minutes. The collected data is sent to the same server over plain HTTP on port 8080. A total of 94 compromised repositories with the second-stage component have been identified. As for the second CI workflow, it's the same as the original malicious workflow, but with added credential formats to look for and a fallback that uploads findings to a secret GitHub gist if the POST fails. The second workflow goes by the following names - lint.yml ci-check.yml build-check.yml repo-health.yml audit.yml code-review.yml test-suite.yml cache-cleanup.yml OpenSourceMalware said the 94 repositories belong to 66 owners, out of which 15 have since been deleted, renamed, or made private. Of the still accessible repositories, most of them appear to have been largely abandoned, with one of them left untouched for more than nine years. Sixty-five of the 79 went without a commit for more than a year. "Stage 1 needs GitHub to run the workflow," OpenSourceMalware said. "On October 9, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running, and the waves on October 10 and 12 extracted no secrets. Stage 2 adds a launcher that doesn't need a runner at all, and it arrived six days after the block. We can’t say the block caused it. We can say the operator moved to a place GitHub's controls don't reach." To mitigate the threat, developers should revoke GitHub access and tokens from a clean device, change their passwords, audit their repositories, rotate every credential the workflows can reach, and alert users who have cloned the repositories. "We don't know who the operator is, but their work suggests limited experience," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, told The Hacker News. "The stealer's environment-variable filter misses most API keys, its home-directory search can time out and discard its own results, and a single IP handles exfiltration, phishing, and noisy internet scanning. That last mistake is why searching for the IP still finds infections."

194m92b.text: In Salesforce Agentforce, the recommended way to make an agent respond to events is a Flow: a record is created or a case is updated, and the Flow passes data into the agent's prompt. Separately, Email-to-Case and Web-to-Case turn inbound customer messages into case records; it is how airlines and hotels run support intake. Both are standard, documented, as-designed features. Chained together, they produce this path: public internet → email → case record → agent prompt → agent action → case comment → outbound reply An unauthenticated outsider now has a route into an internal agent's instructions, and the agent's reply leaves through the same door. Nothing was misconfigured. The finding, documented by researchers in August 2026, is a clean example of how agents that arrive inside existing platforms fail: through the application around them, not the model inside them. The risk is in the application, and the application is the thing nobody re-reviewed Which intake features are enabled, which triggers fire, which objects are exposed to guest users, which automation passes untrusted data where, and which model version the agent is quietly calling underneath: these are the variables that decide whether the Agentforce chain is a support-queue nuisance or a data exposure. A vendor risk review performed once at procurement sees none of them, because the agent did not exist at procurement. A prompt filter watching the agent's inputs does not know that a particular input originated from a stranger, because prompt filters do not understand Email-to-Case. Securing an inherited agent therefore means understanding its host application at the depth its own admins do. That depth is the one thing a questionnaire and a scanner both lack. The City-Forum campaign, an active worldwide data-theft operation against Salesforce and ServiceNow instances running since March 2025, was found in exactly this territory: the gap between platform features and the configurations enterprises actually run. Builders are multiplying, and some of them are agents The platforms have made agent creation as accessible as making a slide deck. Marketing operations builds an agent to pull pipeline reports. Finance builds one to reconcile invoices. Each rides its creator's permissions, because that is what makes it useful. Shadow AI was an employee pasting data into a chatbot. Shadow agents are that employee's access, running unattended, multiplied across everything they were ever granted. Increasingly, agents also build agents. A coding agent tagged into a chat channel can scaffold and deploy another agent as easily as it opens a pull request; an orchestration platform spins up sub-agents to divide a task, each with its own connections and none with its own review. Any governance model that assumes a human requested each agent is quietly obsolete. Why governance keeps producing a document Ask a large enterprise about agent governance and the answer is usually a document: an acceptable-use policy, a monthly committee, a set of principles nobody disputes and nothing enforces. Ask the operational question, how many agents are running right now, what can they reach, and who owns each one, and the document does not know. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 now describes the sharpest version of this gap under its "No Governance" category: a skill deployed and managed inside a third-party platform is unreachable by external scanners (OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 whitepaper, ast10-top10-whitepaper-2, published at owasp.github.io). The tools an enterprise points at the problem from outside cannot see inside the venues where most agents live. Governance fails most often because the rules get written before the security team can see the things the rules apply to. The stack, bottom-up, with a test for each layer The working order is bottom-up, and each layer is the precondition for the one above it. A practical way to check whether a program is real is to apply an operational test at each level. Layer What it has to produce The operational test Discovery A continuously refreshed population across app configs, OAuth grants, network, endpoint, email metadata, and browser Is the discovered count several multiples of the list IT keeps? If not, discovery isn't reaching where agents live. Posture Every platform's agent-relevant settings, measured against how they should be configured Can the team list the intake features and guest-user exposures wired to agent triggers on its top three platforms? Identity and ownership An identity and a named owner per agent, with a lifecycle Pick an agent at random. Does a human raise a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" Usage Who is building what, through which surface, with what data Is there a sanctioned path that ships a business team's agent with secure defaults, or only a block? Agent controls Least privilege against observed need, approval and quarantine for new agents, risk tiering that reflects each agent's full context Does the same finding on a sandboxed dev agent and a customer-facing one show different severities? Runtime Live inspection and intervention Is it fed by the five layers above, or deployed first and enforcing blind? The cost of paper compliance The EU AI Act's penalties carry GDPR-level weight: up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for other violations. Every framework converging on it assumes the stack above exists. GDPR already showed what happens when it does not. British Airways (£20 million) and Marriott (£18.4 million) were not fined for having imperfect policies. Everyone has imperfect policies. They were fined because compliance existed on paper and could not be evidenced operationally when regulators asked. A governance practice built bottom-up generates that evidence as a byproduct: the inventory, the owners, the configurations, the review history. Some platforms are designed to produce exactly that record. One leading example is Reco, which discovers agents across multiple vantage points, including the ones that never touch SSO, and assigns each a risk profile before any policy can be applied to it. The Agentforce chain at the top of this article is not an exploit. It is a configuration, and configurations are governable, provided someone can see them. Chapters 1 to 3 of Into the Expanse cover the shift, the three launch vectors, and the governance practice in full: https://www.reco.ai/agent-ecosystem-security

15qjr4s.text: A fake Web3 accelerator has been observed pushing information stealers and backdoors to Windows and macOS systems using malicious npm packages under the pretext of offering free artificial intelligence (AI) credits for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini, coding tools, and security audits. "The tools delivered information-stealing malware and backdoors for macOS and Windows machines," Elastic Security Labs researchers Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic said. "The operation also repackaged a legitimate coding agent to send model requests through attacker-controlled services, while its audit tools generated fabricated security findings." The scheme poses as a Web3 venture capital accelerator named Apex Accelerator to target cryptocurrency startups and founders. It's being tracked under the moniker REF8801. The names of the npm packages, each of which targets both Windows and macOS machines, are listed below - @apexacc/cli (Apex Copilot CLI — AI advisor for Web3 founders) - @apexacc/audit (Web3 Security Scanner — 18 tools for DYOR and smart contract auditing) While both the packages and their associated GitHub repositories are no longer accessible, "@apexacc/cli" was advertised as an "AI advisor for Web3 founders" that's powered by Claude Fable 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. "@apexacc/audit," on the other hand, claimed to be a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing 18 security tools for scanning tokens, wallets, and smart contracts. Both packages were published by an npm user named "apexaccelerator" and linked to a GitHub account called "apexaccs" and an entity referred to as the Apex Foundation. Interestingly, the campaign itself is not new. In late July 2026, SafeDep detailed three other npm packages linked to the same operation that were found distributing a macOS stealer belonging to the Atomic Stealer (aka AMOS) family - @apexfdn/apex @copilot-mcp/apex, which features the same package description as "@apexacc/cli" @apexfdn/copilot-mcp, which claims to be an Apex Copilot and MCP server for "portfolio diligence and operator tools" Artifacts captured by Socket show that the Apex Foundation has been linked to at least two distinct domains since April 2026 apexaccs[.]org apexfdn[.]xyz According to Internet Archive snapshots dating back to March 19, 2026, the foundation states: "The Apex Foundation offers $235,000 investments, grants, and partnerships, and connects projects with VCs, angels, and private equity if they don't meet our criteria." Posts shared on X show the accelerator approaching developers of cryptocurrency wallets and market intelligence tools for traders with offers of direct investment and instructions to run their due diligence tool ("@apexacc/cli"). In the case of the latter, the npm package has been found to drop an encrypted malware loader disguised as an Apple app ("com.apple.system.loader"). "The group also sought to build credibility through its presence at TOKEN2049 in Singapore and other in-person events it has hosted in the past," Elastic said. "The group attempts to manufacture legitimacy by appearing at widely attended conferences, indirectly lending credibility to the project." Once installed, neither of the npm packages provides the promised functionality. The 18 security tools part of the @apexacc/audit package generate fabricated findings, while @apexacc/cli's scoring test returns an unsupported assessment of a fictitious project. Instead, their primary responsibility is to propagate a macOS backdoor called CloudSyncD and a custom Windows information stealer that exfiltrates data through Telegram. The platform-specific executables are retrieved from the projects' GitHub releases. Both packages implement a distinct verification path for Windows and macOS by sending an HTTP POST request to "win32" or "darwin" to "vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf" to initiate the appropriate next stage. The Windows and macOS infection chains are as follows - Windows - The malware retrieves a Base64-encoded PowerShell command, which reaches out to another endpoint ("0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService") to fetch a second PowerShell script ("drop.ps1") that downloads an executable ("bludness.exe") from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu" and launches it in a hidden window. The PyInstaller executable is a Python loader that checks if it already has administrator privileges and, if so, downloads the next stage from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu," saves it as "%TEMP%\exegis.exe," and launches it. If not, it attempts to bypass User Account Control (UAC) using UACME's ucmDebugObjectMethod(). The "exegis.exe" binary is another PyInstaller executable that collects system metadata, running processes, and performs anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks before decrypting and launching a bundled loader as "%TEMP%\updater_loader.exe." The Golang executable patches Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), unhooks "ntdll.dll" to blind endpoint security tools, and loads the next-stage shellcode into its own memory. The shellcode is a native information stealer that examines for signs of a prior infection and then harvests system information, clipboard text, process listings, Wi-Fi profile names, screenshots, and data from wallets, browser extensions, messengers, remote-access and file transfer protocol (FTP) applications, virtual private network (VPN) clients, browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and Yandex), and game clients. The stealer can also bypass Chrome's app-bound encryption (ABE) protections to extract saved passwords, session cookies, browsing history, download records, and profile metadata. The collected data is exfiltrated through Telegram. macOS - The malware downloads a remotely hosted bash script and executes it on the machine. The shell script downloads a GZIP-compressed archive from "verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/," saves it as "package.tar.gz" in a temporary directory, and extracts its contents. The archive contains a dropper for CloudSyncD, which first phishes the victim's system login password using a fake authorization prompt and then uses it to launch an embedded payload with sudo privileges. The payload performs host discovery, collects hardware and operating-system details, and then contacts an external server ("ccmihr[.]com") to transmit the data and receive further tasks that allow the malware to download and run additional payloads. It's worth noting that CloudSyncD was first documented by Jamf Threat Labs late last month, detailing its propagation via a fake Zoom installer. The malware was detected in the wild in mid-September 2026. "Its behaviors illustrate how macOS malware continues to move toward native implementations, string protection, and execution paths that attempt to avoid writing payloads to disk, while still depending on the oldest technique available: asking the user for their password," Jamf said. Besides deploying a stealer and backdoor depending upon the infected operating system, the packages are capable of intercepting and redirecting OpenRouter large language model (LLM) traffic, as well as registering an MCP server under their control in the victim's agent configuration. "These changes allow the attacker-controlled API to receive the prompts, conversation history, code snippets, and tool outputs included in the agent's LLM requests," Elastic researchers explained. "The attacker's MCP server can also supply instructions that are added to the agent's prompt, along with tool names, descriptions, and accepted inputs that help the model decide which tools to invoke and how to use them. Together, these mechanisms give the attacker visibility into the submitted data and a way to influence the agent's subsequent actions."

1gxrqwp.text: A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16. He showed the attack working against home gateways supplied by three Belgian internet providers, in one case reading the Wi-Fi password off the device and in another opening a remote shell over the air. No CVE has been assigned to the flaw, and no fix has been deployed to the affected routers, Kaiser says. The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in. Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory. From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it. Against an Orange Belgium gateway, the Askey TCG3000 read the Wi-Fi password (the PSK) from the router's stored settings, sent it back over the air, and then joined the network with it. Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed. Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says. He reports no real-world attacks using the flaw. The working exploits are his own. What's Affected Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected. The vulnerable chips fall into two families: older eCos-based models (the BCM3380, BCM3383 and BCM33834), where he found no usable fix and calls the bug a permanent "forever day," meaning a flaw that will never be patched on those devices, and newer Linux-based models (the BCM3390, BCM65xx and BCM68xx), which could be fixed if their makers switch Wi-Fi software. In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO. A fourth, Telenet, may be affected too, but he could not test one. A wider list he published, ranging from Cisco small-business access points to Huawei and ARRIS routers, mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries, and some rest on an automated check that only flags a device as "likely vulnerable." The Belgian per-provider counts, he says, run into the hundreds of thousands of gateways, but are rough estimates. Why There's No Patch, and No CVE The flaw is old. Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix. On the older eCos chips, he says, no working fix was ever shipped, which is why he calls it a forever day. No CVE, the tracking identifier that lets defenders and vendors follow a flaw, has been assigned to it. Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched. When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so. The Hacker News found no CVE for the flaw as of October 19. What Defenders Can Do There is no patch to install, and no setting Kaiser points to that blocks the attack over the air. What he provides instead is a way to find affected gear: YARA rules that spot the vulnerable code in extracted firmware, and a script that listens to a live access point and reports whether it looks vulnerable. Both are triage aids, he notes: a patched device can still match the rules, so a hit is a reason to check further, not a confirmed finding. For gear that will never be fixed, replacement is the practical option. Kaiser frames the bug as well suited to attackers who reach a target over nearby Wi-Fi rather than the internet, a technique Russian state hackers have used to breach networks from across the street.

ffnn48.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 19, 2026Data Breach / Artificial Intelligence An intruder reached a legacy system at OpenCode on the night of October 16 and may have exposed the third-party AI provider keys that users had saved in OpenCode Console, the company said. Console is OpenCode's optional hosted service: a workspace saves its own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key there, and Console uses that key to call the provider so team members can use the models without ever seeing the key. The affected group is 1.4% of Console users, all of whom have an outside provider linked, and OpenCode has told them via email to revoke those keys with each provider and replace them. The email went out on the morning of October 17 under the subject line "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." Anyone who did not get one was not affected, OpenCode said in a post on X later that day. The keys at risk are the ones pasted into Console. The OpenCode command-line and desktop apps keep provider keys added on the machine in a SQLite database there. The breach involves "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself," co-founder Dax Raad wrote in a reply on X, and those keys "never come to us." A provider key is a bearer credential: whoever holds a copy can run billable requests against the owner's account until the provider revokes it. Deleting the key from Console does not revoke it, and a Console budget cannot cap that use either, because Console only sees requests that pass through its own gateway. For a key that was saved in a Console workspace, OpenCode's email and the providers' own guidance give these steps: Revoke the key in the provider's own dashboard and create a new one, following the instructions from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. Update every application and script that used the old key. Review usage and billing at the provider for requests you did not make, going back at least to October 16. OpenCode has not said when the unauthorized access began. Set a spend limit or alert at the provider and give each tool its own key, so a copied key does less damage and its use is easier to trace. Some users say they have already paid for usage they did not run. Dealroom reported that Colin Parsons wrote on X that his OpenAI key had been used for $281 and his Anthropic key for $168, and that Preston Zeller put his losses at $1,700. Notebookcheck reported a Reddit user's claim of $400 of unauthorized usage on an Anthropic account, and another's of about €200 of Google usage, with the project then suspended. Those are the users' own accounts. OpenCode's own wording is that the keys "may have been exposed," and it has not said that any key was copied or used. OpenCode's October 17 post also called the incident ongoing, said the company was working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to fix it, and described the breach as "related to a large-scale distillation attack." The company has not named anyone or said how the two connect, what the legacy system was, how it was reached, how many keys it held, or how many users 1.4% represents. Distillation is the term AI model providers use for campaigns that pull a model's answers in huge numbers to train a rival model. Anthropic said in September that the labs behind such campaigns reach its models through networks of fake accounts created with stolen credit cards, login credentials and harvested API keys. A stolen key has other uses too: criminal markets resell AI tokens and keys and use them to run up bills. Attackers were still trying to get into OpenCode's systems on October 18, Raad wrote on X: they had been "non stop trying to attack our systems for the past 48 hours," and "a side effect is everything is getting hardened."

shs9gu.text: ConnectWise on Saturday said it has disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The disabled identities are listed below - ConnectWise Cloud Backup - 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae ConnectWise Cloud Management - 2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83 ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams - 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online - b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519 ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph - 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center - 412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online - b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. "Disabling the affected connections prevents new authentication through those connections; it does not reverse changes previously made inside a tenant," it said. "The affected shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid. Previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire or are otherwise invalidated. Any unauthorized credentials, permissions, or other access established through separate identities require additional review and remediation." ConnectWise also noted that scheduled backups are not running, and access to affected backup archives and restoration capabilities remains unavailable. However, it emphasized that existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, and that there is no evidence they were breached or accessed by the attackers. Out of an abundance of caution, the company said it has temporarily taken SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline while it completes its review of the incident. Furthermore, the company revealed that it identified the issue on October 14, 2026, through its "advanced cybersecurity monitoring and diligence," prompting it to activate internal and external incident investigation and response actions. "Since implementing these mitigations, we have not observed successful threat activity in the environments we monitor," it said. "This finding does not establish the status of downstream customer environments, which, by design, we cannot directly observe." At this stage, it's unclear if a product vulnerability contributed to the compromise of the application identities. The exact credential-exposure mechanism is the subject of an ongoing analysis, ConnectWise added. The attack is particularly dangerous as it allows an attacker to abuse the application's credentials to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without having to steal each customer's password individually. By using the stolen application credential to authenticate as that application, the attacker can request access tokens from Microsoft Entra ID based on the application's existing permissions. Depending on the permissions assigned to the application, this could enable the attacker to potentially access other Microsoft services, including mailboxes, SharePoint documents, Teams messages, and directory information. With ConnectWise's applications operating with extensive permissions to perform backups and management tasks, the theft of the credential allows the threat actor to authenticate as the application itself and expand their access by adding it to the Global Administrator role, adding client secrets to other trusted applications in the tenant, and creating new applications and granting them permissions. By doing so, the client secrets offer a way to authenticate as that application and establish persistence, providing an alternative means to regain access to the compromised environment even if the original compromised credential is later revoked. Second, Targeted Wave of Attempts Observed "We last observed malicious sign-ins from the original address on October 15 at 08:45 UTC, with targeted, manual activity continuing until about 14:20 UTC that day," Jon Semon, Principal Security Operations Analyst at Huntress, told The Hacker News. "ConnectWise has said access to Cloud Backup is shut off, and if so, activity through that service should have stopped. However, if the threat actor was able to add credentials to applications in Microsoft tenants, those credentials would let them keep access and act as the application." Huntress said it has not identified new malicious activity since October 15, but there is no evidence that the stoppage was the result of public disclosure. "We have high confidence the threat actor also targeted the ConnectWise Cloud Management apps for Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and SharePoint, and we have confirmed abuse of the Teams app in one tenant," Semon said. "Those apps do not appear to have been disabled by ConnectWise, so additional activity could come from them, and we are actively investigating." As of late Saturday, Huntress said it identified a "second, targeted wave of attempts" from the IP address "144.172.64[.]128" on October 15. These efforts, which singled out a narrow scope of 16 tenants, were unsuccessful. The tenants are in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors. "For the new target set, the first sweep targeted Graph tokens from the SkyKick app and occurred on October 15 between 09:25:04 and 12:35:50 UTC," Huntress said. "The second sweep hit the same tenants on the same date, between 13:54:39 and 14:20:24 UTC. This sweep appeared to be manual and targeted Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs." In all, the managed security service provider has identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address associated with the unauthorized activity from the IP address in question, out of which 300 succeeded. Despite the successful sign-in, the absence of a service principal in some tenants is said to have prevented the threat actor from gaining access to those tenants. Partners are advised to take the following actions - Review both their own Microsoft 365 tenant and each managed customer tenant, including environments with dormant SkyKick connections. Verify the status of the listed application connections and keep affected applications disabled until further notice. Review sign-ins across identities from October 13, 2026, through the current time, specifically for activity originating from the IP address "144.172.64[.]128." Preserve available sign-in and audit records before initiating containment steps. Review application and user authentication, application credentials and federation trusts, directory roles, owners, consent grants, and recent policy changes. Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding, inbox or transport rules, and delegated mailbox access. Investigate any other identities changed or used during suspicious activity. "Several Entra controls limit the damage if an application credential is stolen," Huntress said. "Application management policies can restrict or block client secrets on app registrations and cap credential lifetimes. Limiting who holds the Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator roles reduces who can add credentials to applications." "Conditional Access for workload identities, which needs additional licensing, can restrict where an application is allowed to sign in from, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection can flag risky service principals. None of these replace reviewing credentials, but they make a planted secret harder to use or easier to spot."

fxu3ve.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a malicious npm package that's part of a recently disclosed software supply chain attack campaign dubbed MALFEX. The package, named "imgdecode," was uploaded to the package registry on September 30, 2026, by a user named "malfexteste8." It has been downloaded 979 times as of writing and is still available on npm as of writing. The latest version of the package is 1.0.3. "The npm package imgdecode hides a malicious loader in a compiled Node.js addon," SafeDep said. "Its nine-line JavaScript file loads a Windows dynamic-link library (DLL). When a Node.js program calls require('imgdecode') from a Windows console, the DLL attempts to download encrypted shellcode from GitHub. It decrypts the response and injects the result into a new dllhost.exe process." First documented by both Checkmarx and CloudSEK, MALFEX is the name assigned to a long-running campaign in which an unknown threat actor has been publishing malicious packages to npm since August 6, 2023, with an aim to compromise Windows systems. These packages were published across five npm publisher handles: malfexkkj, malfex_user, malfexteste2, malfexteste3, malfexteste4. Of the eight identified packages, three were found to act as a loader for Overlord RAT, while three others ("cdn-img-fetch," "img-to-native," and "native-runner") worked together to download and run a Node.js stealer. A third infection pathway involved the use of a postinstall hook to execute JavaScript capable of contacting an external server and retrieving an unspecified next-stage binary. Interestingly, the threat actor behind the campaign appears to be responding to public disclosures and npm removals by publishing replacements for "native-runner" and "img-to-native" within two days in the form of "runhelper" and "imgbundle." That same day, the first version of "imgdecode" was published. The timeline of events is as follows - September 26, 2026 - cdn-img-fetch, img-to-native, and native-runner 1.0.0 published September 28, 2026, at 4:06 p.m. UTC - npm removes native-runner and img-to-native September 30, 2026, at 3:29 a.m. UTC - imgbundle 1.0.0 published, replacing img-to-native September 30, 2026, at 3:37 a.m. UTC - runhelper 1.0.0 published, replacing native-runner September 30, 2026, at 4:13 p.m. UTC - runhelper unpublished September 30, 2026, at 10:32 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.0 published September 30, 2026, at 11:07 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.1 published October 1, 2026, at 5:48 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.2 published October 7, 2026, at 11:06 p.m. UTC - npm removes imgbundle October 8, 2026, at 1:03 p.m. UTC - npm removes cdn-img-fetch October 11, 2026, at 10:09 p.m. UTC - imgdecode 1.0.3 published The Node.js stealer chain is notable for the fact that none of the packages featured an install hook. Instead, the malicious code runs when "native-runner" is loaded. The package lists "img-to-native" as its dependency, which, in turn, has "img-to-native" as a dependency. The exact functionality of each of these packages is below - cdn-img-fetch downloads "banner.png" from a GitHub repository ("cavecrew/proj") and extracts an encrypted blob. img-to-native decrypts the blob using the key "malfexteam2027" and writes the contents to disk as a Go executable ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\node_runtime_helper.exe"). native-runner executes the Go executable, which then downloads the stealer binary ("setup.exe" aka movinlike) from "104.234.65[.]75:700." "Runhelper," advertised as a helper utility for "launching native binaries from Node.js projects," functions similarly to "native-runner" in that it's designed to run malicious code. Its primary responsibility is to locate a JPG file ("cdn-img-fetch/.runtime/rt.jpg"), extract shellcode from it, copy it into executable memory, and run it using Koffi, a Foreign Function Interface (FFI) module for Node.js. "Six hours after runhelper was unpublished, the operator published imgdecode with a compiled DLL to run the shellcode," SafeDep said. "From version 1.0.1, the DLL also downloads and decrypts the payload. Versions 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 still call require('imgbundle') before loading the DLL. Version 1.0.3 removes that dependency and needs no other MALFEX package." Like in the case of "runhelper," version 1.0.0 of "imgdecode" waits for "imgbundle" to write a file at the location "cdn-img-fetch/.runtime/" and, once it becomes available, reads its contents into memory, and passes them to a native Node.js addon for decoding the data. The addon is a 64-bit Microsoft Visual C++ (MSVC) DLL that first checks if it's running in a developer's terminal, and then proceeds to fetch a JPG file ("banner.jpg") from the same repository ("cavecrew/proj"), decrypt the embedded payload using the key "nif-runtime-2027," and ultimately inject the output into "dllhost.exe." "After decryption, the DLL checks the first bytes of the plaintext," SafeDep explained. "If they match a JPEG or PNG signature, the DLL stops. Inference: the operator could turn the loader off by serving encrypted content that decrypts to an image. Serving an ordinary image would instead generally cause decryption to fail before this check." Although the GitHub account "cavecrew" is no longer accessible, an Internet Archive screenshot of the image file dated October 6, 2026, shows that it's the same Go-based downloader used for retrieving the Node.js stealer and remote access tool ("movinlike") from "104.234.65[.]75:700." The Node.js application includes a .env file containing a command-and-control (C2) address ("104.234.65[.]75:7007") and a MALFEX license key, indicating the use of a malware builder or licensing system to craft such payloads. The malware runs anti-analysis checks that audit for the presence of virtual machines, sandboxes, and analysis tools like Process Monitor and Wireshark, before harvesting files matching seed phrases and specific extensions (.kdbx, .pem, .ppk, and .env), as well as data from Chromium-based web browsers, Discord, Telegram, cryptocurrency wallets, and gaming apps (Steam, Epic Games, Riot, Battle.net, Minecraft, and Ubisoft). It can also establish a WebSocket connection to the C2 server, allowing it to accept commands for shell execution, file transfer, process control, clipboard access, screenshots, and mouse and keyboard input. For persistence, it adds a Registry Run key and creates a scheduled task named "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateService." Developers who have installed any of the aforementioned packages should treat their Windows systems as potentially compromised, isolate them, check for persistence entries, rotate credentials, and transfer funds to new wallets if they seed phrases were stored in them,

kbwmt9.text: Cybersecurity researchers are sounding the alarm related to an active campaign in which unknown threat actors are abusing a compromised Microsoft 365 (M365) credential belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) to gain unauthorized access to customers' M365 environments. ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a cloud-based backup and recovery service built for managed service providers (MSPs) to secure their clients' Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace data. To accomplish its tasks, the application is granted broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data in every tenant on which it's installed. Huntress said it has observed confirmed unauthorized sign-ins within 173 partner/customer tenants using the compromised vendor credential. The incident impacts every organization that has the app installed, and the credential works against every tenant the app is consented in. "The app's credential is in hostile hands," security researcher Jonathan Semon said. "It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list." In the observed attackers, the adversary has been observed authenticating to the app using their own tooling, in a manner analogous to the backup service, and obtains tokens with the app's existing permissions. Given that the app has extensive permissions to access customer data, an attacker in possession of the tokens can read mailboxes, files, and directory data the backup service can. Huntress said the same IP address engaged in password spraying against four law firm tenants on October 13 and 14, 2026, although it said it detected no successful user sign-ins in its telemetry. In at least one partner tenant, the cybersecurity company said it found a separate ConnectWise app assigning itself Global Administrator privileges and adding credentials to other trusted applications within this environment, thereby opening a pathway to other privileged apps within customer environments. This effectively extends the risk beyond the vendor account. "The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) added itself to the Global Administrator role, then ran a Python script (User-Agent Python-urllib/3.12) that modified two other applications in the tenant: an MSP management application, and Huntress's own application (Huntress Security Platform), adding new client secrets to both," Semon explained. "The two applications that received new secrets are trusted, privileged tools. Adding a credential to an MSP management application can extend access beyond the one tenant, because those applications are often consented into the MSP's customers' tenants. A credential on a security tool's application gives the holder whatever that tool is permitted to do." Todyl, in a similar analysis, said it detected an unauthorized party authenticating to Microsoft Graph as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. "The access inherited the app's existing consent, which permits read/write access to mail and attachments (full mailbox access through Exchange Web Services), OneDrive and SharePoint files, and Teams chats, including the ability to restore data," Nicholas Koken, Todyl's head of Detection Engineering, said. "Revoking user sessions does not end this access. Disabling the app in a tenant stops new tokens from being issued there, though tokens already issued stay valid for up to 90 minutes. Any tenant where the app is still enabled stays exposed until ConnectWise rotates the credential." In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of closing Cloud Backup application access until further notice. The company said it has found no evidence that Cloud Backup partner backup data has been compromised. It has also shared the following steps to look for indicators of compromise - In the Microsoft Entra Admin Center, navigate to Monitoring → Sign-in logs, select the Service principal sign-ins tab, and filter by Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. The default User sign-ins tab will not display the required information. In the IP address column, review authentication activity originating from IP addresses outside expected Microsoft/Azure ranges. The application's normal egress has been identified as Azure private IPv6. Suspicious IP address: 144.172.64[.]128 "The backup service needs broad access to do its job, and an attacker using its credentials will inherit that level of access for every tenant where the app is installed," Huntress explained. "Depending on the permissions in the tenant, that can include mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information, much of it belonging to your clients. Some of that access, such as directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail, which is why we suggest acting now instead of waiting for proof of access. The full potential impact depends on the permissions in play in each tenant." Users are recommended to disable the application until ConnectWise confirms all credentials have been reset, enable Microsoft Graph activity logs, audit for any new credentials added since October 13, 2026, and check Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to a directory role. The development comes as Google's Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group, along with ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab, detailed an "ephemeral supply chain tampering" of the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Backupper, a data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery software, to bypass traditional security defenses and deliver malware such as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD. "The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers," Google said. "Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates." The ZIP archive contains CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging follow-on payloads. It's also designed to establish scheduled task-based persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework for covert command-and-control, via DLL sideloading. The software supply chain compromise campaign, which occurred between April and July 2026, has been attributed to a previously undocumented threat cluster codenamed UNC7017. The activity marks the first time that such a compromise has played out in brief intervals instead of maintaining a persistent, static modification on the servers. The campaign is assessed to have impacted organizations spanning a wide range of sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education, and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the U.S. An Active Supply Chain Attack In a post on X, Microsoft said it's tracking an "active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens across customer tenants." The tech giant said the threat actor likely abused permissions previously granted by customers to the application, including highly privileged permissions like Directory.ReadWrite.All. "On October 15, 2026, we observed broad successful service principal authentication originating from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128," it added. "Follow-on activity included Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials on the related service principal in target tenants to maintain direct access as a backdoor." Microsoft is recommending that security teams review service principal sign-ins from unrecognized IP addresses, app credential changes, and OAuth grant activity associated with the aforementioned OAuth AppId. ConnectWise, in a separate advisory, confirmed it has identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment. It has shut off Cloud Backup application access while its "investigation and remediation efforts remain ongoing." (This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

39bjr.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 16, 2026Vulnerability / OpenBSD A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September. The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018, shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix. The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix. No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks. The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it. The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643.
